Both encrypt the entire payload, but RADIUS cannot perform accounting and TACACS+ cannot perform authorization
RADIUS is used only for wired switch ports, and TACACS+ is used only for wireless networks and VPN gateways
TACACS+ uses TCP, encrypts the whole payload and separates authentication, authorization and accounting; RADIUS uses UDP and encrypts only the password
questions.explanation: TACACS+ uses TCP, separates the AAA functions and encrypts the full payload, making it popular for device administration. RADIUS uses UDP, combines authentication and authorization, and encrypts only the password. The other statements reverse or invent characteristics.

questions.question: A company deploys WPA2-Personal using a single pre-shared key known to all employees. A departing employee still knows the key. Which change BEST improves accountability and offboarding?
options: Enable MAC address filtering on all access points and keep the shared key
Reduce the transmit power of the access points so the signal barely leaves the building
Move to WPA2 or WPA3 Enterprise with 802.1X and individual credentials
Hide the SSID so that the network cannot be discovered
questions.explanation: Enterprise mode authenticates each user individually, so access can be revoked per person and actions are attributable. Hiding the SSID, MAC filtering and power reduction offer little protection because they are easily bypassed.

questions.question: Which protocol provides authentication and integrity for IP packets but NOT encryption?
options: Secure Shell (SSH)
IPsec Authentication Header (AH)
IPsec Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP)
Transport Layer Security (TLS)
questions.explanation: AH authenticates and protects integrity of the packet but does not encrypt. ESP can provide confidentiality in addition, and TLS and SSH encrypt data at other layers.

questions.question: Remote staff use full-tunnel VPN connections. Network teams propose enabling split tunneling to reduce bandwidth use at headquarters. What is the MOST significant security concern?
options: Internet traffic bypasses corporate inspection, and a compromised device can bridge it to the internal network
VPN encryption will no longer work for the traffic that is sent to internal applications
The VPN gateway will lose its certificate and users will see repeated trust warnings
Internal DNS servers will stop resolving the names of internal applications for remote users
questions.explanation: Split tunneling removes the corporate security stack from internet traffic and exposes a dual-homed endpoint. Encryption of the internal flows still works, and certificates and DNS are unaffected by this change.

questions.question: A web application firewall (WAF) would MOST directly protect against which threat?
options: ARP spoofing on an internal switch used by the office users
Physical theft of the web server from the data center rack
Unencrypted Telnet sessions from administrators to a core router
SQL injection and cross-site scripting against a web application
questions.explanation: A WAF inspects HTTP traffic at the application layer to block attacks such as injection and scripting. ARP spoofing is a Layer 2 issue, physical theft is a physical control matter, and Telnet exposure is a protocol choice.

questions.question: A DNS administrator wants resolvers to be able to verify that the DNS records they receive have not been tampered with. Which technology provides this?
options: A split-horizon DNS configuration
Dynamic DNS
DNSSEC
DNS over HTTPS
questions.explanation: DNSSEC digitally signs records so that resolvers can validate their authenticity and integrity. DNS over HTTPS encrypts queries but does not prove the data is genuine, split-horizon serves different answers internally and externally, and dynamic DNS updates records automatically.

questions.question: Customers receive phishing emails that appear to come from the company's own domain. The company wants receiving mail servers to reject unauthenticated messages claiming to be from its domain. Which combination is MOST effective?
options: Training customers to inspect the sender display name and hover over links
SPF and DKIM, with a DMARC policy of quarantine or reject
TLS encryption for all outbound mail to partner and customer servers
A larger spam filter at the company's own mail gateway to catch inbound phishing
questions.explanation: SPF and DKIM authenticate the sending infrastructure and message, and DMARC instructs receivers on handling failures. TLS protects transport, not domain impersonation, internal spam filters do not affect other people's inboxes, and training alone is not a technical control.

questions.question: A switch port in a public conference room should provide network access only to authenticated company devices that meet a minimum patch level. Which technology fits?
options: 802.1X with network access control and posture assessment
A static VLAN assignment for the conference room's switch ports
A longer DHCP lease time for guest devices in the room
Port mirroring to a monitoring system on the conference room switch
questions.explanation: 802.1X authenticates the device or user before granting access, and NAC can evaluate posture. A static VLAN permits any device that plugs in, and DHCP and mirroring do not authenticate anything.

questions.question: Which layer of the OSI model do routers primarily operate at, and which addressing do they use?
options: Layer 2, the data link layer, using MAC addresses
Layer 4, the transport layer, using port numbers
Layer 1, the physical layer, using signals
Layer 3, the network layer, using IP addresses
questions.explanation: Routers forward packets between networks based on IP addresses at Layer 3. Switches typically work with MAC addresses at Layer 2, transport protocols use ports at Layer 4, and Layer 1 handles signaling over media.

questions.question: A company hosts customer-facing services that were taken down by a very large flood of traffic from thousands of hosts. Which mitigation is MOST effective against this type of attack?
options: Blocking the single source IP address responsible for most of the packets
Adding stricter password rules to the web application's customer login page
Disabling ICMP on the internal switches and routers in the data center
Upstream traffic scrubbing or a CDN that absorbs and filters the flood
questions.explanation: A distributed attack cannot be stopped by blocking one source; upstream providers and CDNs with large capacity can absorb and filter the traffic. Passwords and internal ICMP settings are irrelevant to volumetric floods.

questions.question: A global retailer is considering SD-WAN with a cloud-delivered security stack including secure web gateway, firewall as a service and zero trust network access. Which term describes this convergence?
options: A Type 2 hypervisor running on a host operating system
Network address translation at the perimeter router
Secure access service edge (SASE)
A demilitarized zone between two firewalls
questions.explanation: SASE combines wide-area networking with cloud-delivered security services. A DMZ is a screened network segment, a Type 2 hypervisor is virtualization software, and NAT translates addresses.

questions.question: Which statement about TLS 1.3 compared with older versions is correct?
options: It relies on SSL 3.0 for its record layer to remain compatible with older browsers
It removed legacy cipher suites and requires forward secrecy via ephemeral key exchange
It permits RC4 and CBC cipher suites for backward compatibility with legacy clients
It uses a longer, multi-round handshake to improve security and validate the client
questions.explanation: TLS 1.3 removed weak and legacy options, mandates ephemeral key exchange for forward secrecy and shortens the handshake. SSL is deprecated and not part of it, and RC4 is prohibited.

questions.question: Which TWO measures help defend against VLAN hopping? (Choose two.)
options: Use the native VLAN for all user traffic
Allow all VLANs on every trunk
Enable Telnet on switches for troubleshooting
Disable unused switch ports and place them in an unused VLAN
Disable automatic trunk negotiation on access ports
questions.explanation: Shutting down unused ports and disabling dynamic trunking prevent switch spoofing, and avoiding the native VLAN for user traffic helps prevent double tagging. Allowing all VLANs on trunks and using the native VLAN for user traffic widen the exposure.

questions.question: Which TWO are valid ways to protect email from domain spoofing? (Choose two.)
options: Forcing TLS between the mail server and clients only
Publishing SPF records listing authorized mail servers
Signing outbound mail with DKIM and publishing a DMARC policy
Using a longer password for every mailbox
Adding a disclaimer to the bottom of messages
questions.explanation: SPF, DKIM and DMARC are the standard mechanisms that let receivers verify messages claiming a domain. Longer mailbox passwords, disclaimers and client TLS do not prove a message came from an authorized sender.

questions.question: A security architect is hardening a wireless network. Which TWO changes improve security the MOST? (Choose two.)
options: Deploy wireless intrusion detection to find rogue access points
Hide the SSID
Filter by MAC address only
Use WEP with a long key
Use WPA3 or WPA2-Enterprise with 802.1X
questions.explanation: Strong authentication and encryption, together with monitoring for rogue devices, address the major risks. Hidden SSIDs and MAC filtering are easily defeated, and WEP is broken regardless of key length.

questions.question: Which TWO statements about firewalls are correct? (Choose two.)
options: A firewall protects against threats on the internal network that never cross it
A firewall eliminates the need for patching servers behind it
A stateful firewall tracks the state of connections and permits return traffic for established sessions
A next-generation firewall adds application awareness and intrusion prevention
A stateless packet filter inspects the application payload of every session
questions.explanation: Stateful inspection and next-generation features are standard capabilities. Stateless filters examine headers rather than payload, firewalls cannot see traffic that never crosses them, and they never replace patching.

questions.question: TCP is connection-oriented and reliable, whereas UDP is connectionless and does not guarantee delivery.
questions.explanation: TCP uses a three-way handshake and acknowledgements; UDP is lightweight and leaves reliability to the application.

questions.question: WPA3 uses Simultaneous Authentication of Equals, which improves resistance to offline password guessing compared with WPA2-Personal.
questions.explanation: SAE replaces the WPA2 pre-shared key handshake and resists offline dictionary attacks while providing forward secrecy.

questions.question: DNSSEC encrypts DNS queries so that eavesdroppers cannot see which names are being looked up.
questions.explanation: DNSSEC provides authenticity and integrity of DNS data through signatures, not confidentiality. DNS over HTTPS or TLS encrypts the queries.

questions.question: IPsec ESP in tunnel mode is commonly used to build site-to-site VPNs between gateways.
questions.explanation: Tunnel mode encapsulates the entire original packet inside a new one, and ESP provides confidentiality and integrity, which is the typical gateway-to-gateway configuration.

questions.question: A switch normally operates at Layer 3 of the OSI model and forwards packets using IP addresses.
questions.explanation: Traditional switches operate at Layer 2 using MAC addresses. Routers, and Layer 3 switches, forward using IP addresses at Layer 3.

questions.question: An intrusion prevention system is placed inline and can block malicious traffic, whereas an intrusion detection system typically only monitors and alerts.
questions.explanation: Inline placement lets an IPS drop packets; an IDS usually observes a copy of the traffic and generates alerts.

questions.question: Hiding the SSID of a wireless network is a strong security control that prevents attackers from finding it.
questions.explanation: The SSID is still transmitted in frames and is easily discovered with common tools, so hiding it is not a meaningful security control.

questions.question: A bank requires staff to enter a password and then respond to a security question before reaching the trading application. An auditor says this is not multi-factor authentication. Why?
options: Both checks draw on the same factor category, something the user knows
Security questions are always weaker than passwords and so are not counted
Multi-factor authentication requires a biometric as one of the factors
The two checks happen one after the other rather than at the same moment
questions.explanation: Multi-factor means proof from at least two different categories: know, have or are. A password and a security question are both knowledge, so this is two steps of single-factor authentication. A biometric is not mandatory; a hardware token plus a password qualifies. Sequence is irrelevant, because the factors may be requested in any order.

questions.question: A government lab is choosing between two fingerprint readers. Reader X has a FAR of 0.1% and an FRR of 6%. Reader Y has a FAR of 2% and an FRR of 2%. Which statement is the BEST basis for comparing overall accuracy?
options: Compare each reader's crossover error rate, the point where FAR equals FRR
Choose the reader with the lowest FRR because users will complain less
Choose the reader with the lowest FAR because that is always the only goal
Choose the reader with the highest enrollment time because it is more careful
questions.explanation: The crossover error rate (CER) is the standard single figure for comparing biometric accuracy, because the FAR and FRR can be tuned against each other by changing sensitivity. Picking only the lowest FRR or only the lowest FAR ignores the trade-off; a low FAR may suit a high-security area but not be the best overall accuracy measure. Longer enrollment time says nothing about accuracy.

questions.question: Which authentication approach is MOST resistant to a phishing site that imitates the real login page?
options: A time-based one-time password typed from an authenticator app that refreshes every thirty seconds
A FIDO2 security key bound to the genuine site
A six-digit code delivered by text message to the registered phone
A longer password with required special characters and mixed case
questions.explanation: FIDO2/WebAuthn credentials are tied to the real site origin, so a look-alike domain cannot obtain a valid response, and there is no secret to type. TOTP codes and SMS codes can be relayed by a phishing proxy in real time. A stronger password still gets handed over to the fake page.

questions.question: In a Kerberos realm, a user has already authenticated and now wants to use the file server. Which component issues the ticket for that specific service?
options: The authentication service in the key distribution center, which verifies the password again
The file server itself, using the user's clear-text credentials stored locally
The ticket-granting service, in exchange for the ticket-granting ticket
The certificate authority that signed the user's certificate during enrollment
questions.explanation: After the AS issues a TGT, the user presents it to the ticket-granting service in the KDC, which returns a service ticket for the file server without another password prompt. The AS only issues the TGT. Kerberos does not send the password to the service, and a certificate authority belongs to PKI, not to Kerberos ticketing.

questions.question: A network team wants per-command authorization on routers and switches, with the whole administrative session encrypted and a separate authorization step. Which protocol BEST fits?
options: RADIUS
LDAP
Kerberos
TACACS+
questions.explanation: TACACS+ separates authentication, authorization and accounting and encrypts the full payload, which is why it is preferred for device administration with per-command control. RADIUS combines authentication and authorization and encrypts only the password, so it is more typical for network access such as Wi-Fi and VPN. LDAP is a directory protocol, and Kerberos issues tickets for services rather than controlling commands on devices.

questions.question: A hospital lets the owner of each patient-research folder decide who else may open it. Over time, folders end up shared very widely. Which access control model does this describe, and what is its inherent weakness?
options: Mandatory access control, because labels are applied automatically by the system to every folder
Discretionary access control, because owners can pass on access
Role-based access control, because folders map closely to job functions
Rule-based access control, because shared folders follow fixed global rules
questions.explanation: When the resource owner decides who gets access, it is discretionary access control, and that flexibility lets permissions spread beyond what policy intends. Mandatory control uses system-enforced labels and clearances that owners cannot change. Role-based control assigns permissions to roles, not by owner choice, and rule-based control applies global rules to everyone.

questions.question: A company wants contractors to read design documents only if the document is marked "Project Falcon", the contractor works for an approved vendor, the device is compliant, and the request comes during business hours. Which model is the BEST fit?
options: Role-based access control with a separate role for each vendor, device and time window
Discretionary access control managed by each individual document owner
Attribute-based access control evaluating context at request time
Mandatory access control using a military-style classification scheme and clearances
questions.explanation: The decision depends on several attributes at once, including document tag, user affiliation, device health and time, which is exactly what attribute-based control evaluates. Roles cannot express device state or time of day without exploding in number. Discretionary control leaves the decision to owners, and a military-style label scheme does not model these contextual conditions.

questions.question: An employee moves from accounts payable to purchasing and still has the ability to approve vendor payments. Which principle is MOST directly violated, and what process failed?
options: Defense in depth; the penetration testing process failed to find the weakness
Non-repudiation; the digital signature process failed to bind the approver
Fail secure; the system failure handling did not close access when it broke
Separation of duties and least privilege; the mover step failed
questions.explanation: Keeping old rights after a role change is privilege creep, which breaks least privilege and creates a separation-of-duties conflict, because the same person can now both order and approve payments. The failure is in the mover step, where old access should be removed. The other principles describe different problems and do not explain the retained rights.

questions.question: A web application needs to read a user's contacts from a third-party service. The user must not give the application their password for that service. Which standard is designed for this?
options: OAuth 2.0, using an access token with limited scope
SAML 2.0, using a signed assertion about the user
LDAP, using an authenticated bind to the directory
RADIUS, using a shared secret with the network access server
questions.explanation: OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework for delegated access: the user consents, and the application receives a scoped token instead of the password. SAML is mainly for browser single sign-on between organizations, LDAP is a directory access protocol, and RADIUS handles network access authentication. None of them is built for third-party delegated API access.

questions.question: A mobile app team wants users to sign in with their corporate identity and receive a verifiable statement of who the user is. They already use OAuth 2.0 for API access. What should they add?
options: Kerberos tickets issued by an on-premises KDC
OpenID Connect to obtain an ID token
TACACS+ for centralized authorization
A second OAuth scope called "identity" with no other change
questions.explanation: OpenID Connect extends OAuth 2.0 with an ID token that tells the application who authenticated, which is precisely the missing piece. Kerberos is poorly suited to mobile apps across the internet, and TACACS+ is for device administration. OAuth by itself defines no standard way to authenticate the user, so inventing a scope would not be interoperable or verifiable.

questions.question: In a SAML federation between a company and a SaaS vendor, which party creates and signs the assertion about the user?
options: The service provider that hosts the application
The user's web browser, using a stored cookie
The identity provider that authenticated the user
The vendor's certificate authority
questions.explanation: The identity provider authenticates the user and issues a digitally signed assertion, which the service provider validates against the trusted signing certificate. The service provider consumes the assertion; it does not create it. The browser only carries it. A certificate authority may have issued the signing certificate but does not issue assertions.

questions.question: After a merger, the company has dozens of cloud applications and a high helpdesk load from forgotten passwords. Management wants fewer passwords and central enforcement of MFA. What is the BEST step?
options: Allow each business unit to choose its own authentication method and password rules
Force users to rotate every application password every 30 days and add complexity rules
Create a shared service account for each application so staff stop needing passwords
Implement single sign-on through a federated identity provider with MFA
questions.explanation: Single sign-on through a central IdP reduces the number of credentials and gives one place to enforce MFA, conditional policies and fast deprovisioning. Letting units pick their own methods preserves fragmentation. Frequent forced rotation drives weak, reused passwords, and shared accounts destroy accountability.

questions.question: An administrator uses a single shared "admin" password stored in a spreadsheet to maintain production servers. Which control addresses BOTH the credential exposure and the lack of accountability?
options: A privileged access management solution with vaulting, check-out and session recording
A policy requiring the shared password to be at least 20 characters with symbols
A quarterly reminder email telling administrators not to share the password with anyone
A firewall rule limiting administration to the data center network and a jump host
questions.explanation: PAM removes the shared secret from view, ties each use to a named person through check-out, and records what was done, fixing both exposure and attribution. A longer shared password is still shared and unattributable. Reminder emails are not enforceable, and network restriction does not tell you which administrator did what.

questions.question: A user access review finds that 40 people who left the company in the past year still have active accounts in a finance application. Which process improvement addresses the root cause?
options: Increase password complexity requirements for all active accounts in the application
Link account removal to the HR termination event through automation
Move the application behind a more restrictive network firewall
Ask managers to remember to email the helpdesk whenever someone leaves
questions.explanation: The failure is in the leaver step: nothing triggers removal. Tying deprovisioning to the authoritative HR event, ideally with automation such as SCIM, fixes the cause. Stronger passwords and a firewall do nothing about accounts that should not exist. Relying on managers to remember is the manual process that already failed.

questions.question: A company is deploying a badge-controlled server room. An audit finds that employees routinely hold the door open for colleagues behind them. Which physical control BEST prevents this?
options: A mantrap admitting one person at a time
A more visible sign reminding staff to badge in individually at every door
Brighter lighting in the corridor outside the server room door
A longer retention period for badge reader logs and door sensor data
questions.explanation: A mantrap physically enforces single entry and defeats tailgating and piggybacking. Signs and lighting are deterrents that rely on behavior, and longer log retention helps investigations after the fact but does not prevent unauthorized entry.

questions.question: A security architect must decide how to protect an identity provider that all applications depend on. Which risk of single sign-on is MOST important to address in the design?
options: Users will need to remember a larger number of separate passwords
Applications will no longer be able to log individual user activity
The identity provider becomes a single point of failure and prime target
Users will not be able to use multi-factor authentication at all
questions.explanation: Centralizing authentication concentrates both availability risk and attacker interest, so the design needs high availability, strong MFA and monitoring on the IdP. SSO reduces rather than increases the number of passwords, applications can still log activity, and MFA is typically easier to enforce centrally.

questions.question: Which two statements about OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect are correct? (Choose two.)
options: OAuth 2.0 is a framework for delegated authorization using access tokens
OpenID Connect adds an identity layer, issuing an ID token about the authenticated user
OAuth 2.0 transmits the user's password to the relying application
OpenID Connect replaces TLS by encrypting tokens itself
OAuth 2.0 assertions are XML documents signed by the identity provider
questions.explanation: OAuth 2.0 gives applications scoped access tokens, and OpenID Connect layers authentication on top by issuing an ID token. OAuth specifically avoids handing the password to the relying app. OpenID Connect depends on TLS and does not replace it, and XML assertions describe SAML, not OAuth.

questions.question: Which two controls BEST reduce the risk of privilege creep? (Choose two.)
options: Periodic access recertification by managers and data owners
Removing prior access as part of every role change (the mover step)
Allowing users to request any access they think they may need later
Giving every employee the same standard permission set at hire
Extending password lifetimes to reduce helpdesk contacts
questions.explanation: Creep is the buildup of access nobody removed, so reviews that confirm each entitlement and a mover process that strips old rights are the direct fixes. Allowing speculative requests or broad default sets increases unnecessary access, and password lifetime has no bearing on entitlements.

questions.question: Which two items are examples of "something you have" authentication factors? (Choose two.)
options: A hardware token that displays a rotating code
A smart card with an embedded certificate
A four-digit personal identification number
A retina pattern
The user's mother's maiden name
questions.explanation: Tokens and smart cards are physical possessions, the Type 2 category. A PIN and a maiden name are knowledge factors, and a retina pattern is an inherence (something you are) factor.

questions.question: A company evaluates controls to enforce separation of duties in its payment process. Which two are appropriate? (Choose two.)
options: The person who creates a vendor cannot approve payments to that vendor
Payments above a threshold require approval from a second authorized person
The accounts payable manager holds every system privilege for convenience
All finance staff share one login to simplify audit trails
Approvers are trusted so their activity is not logged
questions.explanation: Splitting vendor creation from payment approval and requiring a second approver for large payments both prevent one person from completing a fraud alone. Combining all privileges in one person is the opposite, shared logins destroy accountability, and unlogged approvers remove the detective control.

questions.question: A user who must enter a password and the answer to a personal security question has been authenticated with two factors.
questions.explanation: Both items are knowledge factors, so this is single-factor authentication used twice. Real multi-factor authentication needs at least two different categories, such as a password and a hardware token.

questions.question: A lower crossover error rate (CER) indicates a more accurate biometric system.
questions.explanation: The CER is where FAR and FRR are equal, so a lower value means the device makes fewer errors of both kinds at its balanced setting. It is the usual single number for comparing biometric products.

questions.question: Under current NIST guidance, forcing all users to change passwords every 60 days is recommended to maintain security.
questions.explanation: NIST SP 800-63B recommends against arbitrary periodic changes, which tend to produce predictable passwords. It favors length, checking against breached lists and MFA, with a change only on evidence of compromise.

questions.question: In mandatory access control, the owner of a file can decide to grant read access to any user they trust.
questions.explanation: That describes discretionary control. In mandatory control the system enforces access from clearance and classification labels, and owners cannot override it.

questions.question: Provisioning access based on role membership still requires a process to remove access when a person changes jobs.
questions.explanation: Role assignment makes granting easier, but unless old role memberships are revoked at the mover step, users accumulate rights. Periodic recertification catches what the process misses.

questions.question: In a Kerberos environment, the user's password is sent across the network each time a service ticket is requested.
questions.explanation: The password is used only to prove identity to the authentication service at the start. After that, tickets are used and the password is not sent to services, which is a major benefit of the design.

questions.question: A retailer is evaluating a payment processor and wants strong assurance that the processor's security controls actually operated effectively over the past year. Which report should the retailer request?
options: A SOC 2 Type I report
A SOC 3 report
A SOC 2 Type II report
A SOC 1 Type I report
questions.explanation: A SOC 2 Type II report tests the operating effectiveness of security-related controls over a period, which is the assurance requested. Type I only describes control design at a single date. SOC 3 is a general-use summary with little detail, and SOC 1 addresses controls over financial reporting rather than security.

questions.question: A manager asks for the cheapest way to learn which servers are missing patches across the data center. Which activity BEST meets this need?
options: A credentialed vulnerability scan
A red-team exercise
A full-scope penetration test
A social engineering test
questions.explanation: A credentialed vulnerability scan logs in to hosts and reports missing patches and weak settings accurately and cheaply. A red-team exercise and a penetration test are slower and costlier and aim to demonstrate exploitation paths, not enumerate every missing patch. Social engineering tests people, not patch levels.

questions.question: Before a penetration test of production systems begins, which item must be obtained FIRST?
options: A list of all vulnerabilities found in the most recent scan of the environment
Written authorization with scope and rules of engagement
Administrator credentials for every system that is in scope for testing
A signed statement from management that no outages are possible
questions.explanation: Written authorization and rules of engagement make the testing legal and define scope, timing and escalation. Past scan results and credentials may be useful later, and no tester can guarantee zero impact, so demanding that guarantee is unrealistic.

questions.question: A tester is given a normal user account and basic network diagrams, then asked to see how far an insider could go. What type of test is this?
options: White box
Gray box
Black box
Blind
questions.explanation: Partial knowledge, such as a user-level account and limited documentation, is gray box testing. White box gives full knowledge including source and architecture, and black box gives none. Blind tests are one where the tester has no information and, in a double-blind variant, the defenders are not told either.

questions.question: A scanner reports a critical vulnerability on an internal server. A senior engineer believes it is a false positive. What should the security analyst do NEXT?
options: Ignore the finding because the senior engineer outranks the scanner's output
Immediately take the server offline to be safe until the vendor responds
Validate the finding by manual verification or another method
Lower the scanner's sensitivity globally to reduce future noise and workload
questions.explanation: Findings should be validated before remediation effort is spent, using manual checks, credentialed verification or another tool. Ignoring it relies on opinion, and taking production offline without validation is disruptive. Lowering sensitivity globally increases the chance of false negatives.

questions.question: Which metric is the BEST example of a key risk indicator for the vulnerability management program?
options: Number of vulnerability scans run each month across all networks
Number of security training slides updated each quarter by the team
Average time analysts spend in meetings about vulnerability reports
Critical vulnerabilities on internet-facing systems past their deadline
questions.explanation: A KRI signals rising exposure, and overdue critical vulnerabilities on exposed systems say how much risk is accumulating. Scan counts and meeting time measure activity, not risk, and training slide updates are unrelated to exposure.

questions.question: A development team wants to find input-handling flaws and crashes in a file parser for which they have no source code. Which technique is MOST appropriate?
options: Fuzzing the parser with malformed files
Static analysis of the source code
Peer review of the design documents
Interviewing the original developers
questions.explanation: Fuzzing sends unexpected or malformed input to a running program and needs no source, which makes it well suited to a closed parser. Static analysis and design review need access to code or documents that are unavailable, and interviews would not find actual defects.

questions.question: The auditors who will report to the board on the effectiveness of the security program must give an unbiased opinion. Which arrangement BEST supports that?
options: Auditors who report to the chief information security officer being audited
Auditors independent of the audited functions, reporting to the board
Auditors who are also responsible for operating the controls under audit
Auditors selected and directed by the managers of the audited departments
questions.explanation: Independence and a reporting line outside the audited function protect objectivity. Reporting to the person being audited, operating the controls they audit, or being chosen by those audited all create conflicts of interest.

questions.question: After a penetration test, the report is a 300-page list of raw scanner output. The CEO asks what it means. What should the security manager have ensured the report contained?
options: A longer list of every informational finding for the sake of completeness
Only the names of the testers, the dates tested and the tools used
An executive summary with prioritized, business-impact-based findings
A promise that all vulnerabilities have now been fixed and verified
questions.explanation: Good reports translate technical results into business risk for the audience and give prioritized recommendations with owners. A longer unfiltered list buries the important issues, names and dates are not findings, and a test cannot promise that everything is fixed.

questions.question: A company wants to verify that its detection tooling would catch common attacker techniques, repeatedly and without scheduling a consultant each time. Which approach BEST fits?
options: An annual internal audit of the policy library
A reciprocal agreement with another company
A single penetration test at year end
Breach and attack simulation tooling run on a schedule
questions.explanation: Breach and attack simulation safely replays attack techniques on a schedule to confirm preventive and detective controls work. A yearly pen test is infrequent, a policy audit does not exercise technical controls, and a reciprocal agreement is a continuity arrangement.

questions.question: A project manager asks whether continuous monitoring can replace the three-year system reauthorization. What is the BEST answer?
options: Yes, it provides ongoing evidence that supports ongoing authorization
No, because monitoring works only for network devices and not for applications
No, because reauthorization is legally required every three years in all cases
Yes, because once a system is authorized it never needs reviewing again
questions.explanation: Information security continuous monitoring supplies near-real-time evidence of control status and risk, supporting ongoing authorization instead of point-in-time snapshots. It is not limited to network devices. Monitoring does not mean no further review, and the assertion of a universal three-year legal requirement is incorrect.

questions.question: A new release has just fixed a security bug in the login module. Which testing activity BEST ensures that later changes do not reintroduce the bug?
options: Regression tests including a case for the fixed flaw
A one-time penetration test of the whole network after release
Increasing the password length requirement for all users
A tabletop exercise for the incident response team next quarter
questions.explanation: Regression tests re-run earlier checks, so adding a test for the specific flaw prevents it from silently returning. A network pen test, password change and tabletop exercise do not protect the code against regression.

questions.question: The security team presents patching statistics to executives. Which presentation is MOST effective?
options: A table listing every host with its patch level and last scan date
A trend of critical systems patched within policy deadlines, with the risk of late ones
The raw output of the patch management console for the whole estate
A walkthrough of how the patch tool works internally and its architecture
questions.explanation: Executives need a measure tied to policy and risk, shown over time and with a clear implication. Raw host tables and console output are too detailed to support decisions, and tool internals do not address risk.

questions.question: An organization wants to confirm that its web application resists abuse by testing scenarios such as bypassing the checkout approval step. Which technique describes this?
options: Misuse case testing
Load testing
Usability testing
Synthetic availability monitoring
questions.explanation: Misuse case testing explores how a feature could be abused and checks that controls hold. Load testing measures performance, usability testing looks at user experience, and synthetic monitoring checks availability and response, none of which target abuse of logic.

questions.question: Which two statements correctly distinguish a vulnerability assessment from a penetration test? (Choose two.)
options: A vulnerability assessment identifies and ranks weaknesses without necessarily exploiting them
A penetration test attempts to exploit weaknesses to show real impact
A vulnerability assessment always requires the testers to have no authorization
A penetration test produces no written report
A vulnerability assessment proves the business impact of chained attacks
questions.explanation: Assessments find and prioritize, while penetration tests prove impact by exploiting. Both need authorization, and a report is the key deliverable of a pen test. Demonstrating chained impact is a penetration-testing strength, not an assessment feature.

questions.question: Which two items belong in the rules of engagement for a penetration test? (Choose two.)
options: Systems and network ranges that are in scope and out of scope
Testing windows and emergency contacts for stopping the test
The personal passwords of the system administrators
A waiver releasing the testers from any reporting duties
A list of production data the testers may copy for their own use
questions.explanation: Rules of engagement set scope, timing, techniques and escalation contacts. Administrators' personal passwords should never be shared, testers must report their findings, and copying production data for personal use would be improper.

questions.question: A SaaS provider offers a SOC 2 Type II report. Which two considerations should a customer reviewing it check? (Choose two.)
options: Whether the audit period and trust criteria cover the services the customer actually uses
Whether exceptions and qualified opinions are noted and understood, including complementary user entity controls
Whether the report is a public marketing summary suitable for broad release
Whether it covers the customer's own internal network controls
Whether it proves that no breach can ever occur
questions.explanation: A SOC 2 report is only as useful as its scope and findings, and the customer must also implement the user entity controls the report assumes. SOC 2 reports are restricted-use, not marketing summaries, and they cover the provider's service rather than the customer's network. No audit proves a breach is impossible.

questions.question: A SOC 2 Type I report provides stronger assurance than a Type II report because it examines the controls in more detail.
questions.explanation: A Type I report covers design at a single point in time. A Type II also tests operating effectiveness over a period, which is stronger assurance.

questions.question: A vulnerability scanner that reports a vulnerability that does not exist has produced a false positive.
questions.explanation: A false positive is a reported problem that is not real. Validation prevents wasted remediation effort.

questions.question: A CVSS base score tells you exactly how much risk a vulnerability poses to your specific organization.
questions.explanation: CVSS expresses the technical severity of a flaw in general. Actual risk depends on your asset value, exposure, existing controls and whether exploitation is occurring.

questions.question: In a gray box test, the tester is given partial knowledge of the target, such as a low-privilege account.
questions.explanation: Gray box sits between black box (no knowledge) and white box (full knowledge), and a user-level account is the usual example.

questions.question: Code coverage of 100 percent guarantees that an application has no security vulnerabilities.
questions.explanation: Coverage only shows how much code the tests executed, not whether they checked security properties or covered unexpected inputs and logic flaws.

questions.question: An internal audit performed by the organization's own staff generally carries more credibility with outside regulators than an audit by an independent external firm.
questions.explanation: External independent audits carry more weight with regulators and customers. Internal audits are valuable for readiness and improvement but are less independent.

questions.question: A responder arrives at a running server suspected of compromise and must preserve evidence for possible prosecution. Which collection order is CORRECT?
options: Disk image first, then memory, then network connections and logs
Memory and running state, then disk, then archived backups
Archived backups first, then disk, then memory and running processes
Shut the server down immediately, then image the disk for analysis
questions.explanation: Evidence is collected from most to least volatile: memory, processes and network state first, then disk, then remote logs and archives. Imaging disk first loses memory contents, and shutting down destroys volatile data that may show the attacker's activity.

questions.question: A forensic analyst copies the contents of a suspect's hard drive for analysis. Which approach is BEST for preserving evidentiary value?
options: Drag and drop the user's folders to an external drive for later review
Use a write blocker to make a bit-for-bit image and verify hash values
Boot the original machine and run a search for suspicious files and tools
Compress the entire drive and email the archive to the analyst
questions.explanation: A write blocker prevents any change to the original, and a bit-for-bit image with matching hashes captures deleted and hidden data and proves the copy is faithful. File copies miss slack and deleted space, booting the original changes it, and emailing an archive breaks custody control.

questions.question: During an investigation, evidence was left in an unlocked cabinet for two days and no record exists of who had access. What is the MOST likely consequence?
options: The evidence becomes more reliable because it was never moved
The hash values will automatically change
The evidence will be treated as classified information
A broken chain of custody may make the evidence inadmissible
questions.explanation: Chain of custody documents who handled the evidence and when. Gaps allow a challenger to argue it could have been altered, risking exclusion. Leaving it unmonitored does not make it more reliable, hashes change only if the data changes, and classification is a different matter.

questions.question: A SIEM generates thousands of low-value alerts daily, and analysts are missing real incidents. What is the BEST improvement?
options: Disable all alerting and review the logs manually once a month
Tune correlation rules and prioritize alerts by asset criticality
Double the number of log sources without changing any of the rules
Reduce log retention so that there is less data to search
questions.explanation: Alert fatigue is solved by tuning and prioritization with context, so analysts see what matters. Disabling alerts removes detection, more sources without tuning adds noise, and shortening retention harms investigations without reducing alerts.

questions.question: Investigators cannot correlate events across a firewall, server and application because timestamps differ by several minutes. Which control would have prevented this?
options: Longer log retention periods on the central collector
Encryption of the log files at rest on each server
More verbose logging levels on the application servers
Synchronizing all systems to a trusted time source
questions.explanation: Correlation depends on consistent timestamps, which comes from synchronization with a trusted source such as NTP. Retention, encryption and verbosity are useful but do not fix clock differences.

questions.question: A company discovers that an administrator edited the logs of a server he manages to hide a configuration change. Which control would BEST have prevented this?
options: Forwarding logs in real time to a store the administrator cannot modify
Increasing the administrator's password length and adding complexity rules
Requiring the administrator to complete annual security awareness training
Rotating the administrator to a different team at the end of each year
questions.explanation: Forwarding logs immediately to a protected central repository, with separation from the people being logged, preserves integrity and accountability. A longer password, training and job rotation might deter or detect later but do not stop log alteration.

questions.question: A security analyst notices that a workstation is communicating with a known malicious address. According to the incident response lifecycle, what is the FIRST action once the event is confirmed as an incident?
options: Rebuild the workstation from a clean image immediately to remove the threat
Publish a press statement to reassure customers and regulators
Update the incident response plan to reflect the new threat
Contain the affected system while preserving evidence
questions.explanation: After detection and analysis confirm an incident, containment limits damage while evidence is preserved. Rebuilding first destroys evidence and may leave the root cause unknown, press statements go through the communications process, and plan updates come in lessons learned.

questions.question: Which phase of incident response is MOST important to complete BEFORE any incident occurs?
options: Eradication
Lessons learned
Preparation
Recovery
questions.explanation: Preparation, meaning the plan, trained team, tools, contacts and logging, determines the quality of everything else and has to be done in advance. The other phases occur during or after an incident.

questions.question: After removing ransomware from several servers, the team wants to bring services back. What should they do to reduce the chance of reinfection?
options: Restore from a known-good backup, after closing the entry vector, and monitor
Restore the most recent backup without checking when the infection began
Reconnect the servers to the network first and scan them afterward while users work
Pay the ransom to make the attacker stop and provide the decryption key
questions.explanation: Recovery should use clean data, with the root cause fixed and heightened monitoring. The latest backup may already be infected, reconnecting before verification invites reinfection, and paying does not guarantee removal or return of data.

questions.question: A change to a production firewall rule caused an outage. The engineer says it was urgent and so no approval was needed. What is the BEST response from the change management perspective?
options: Reward the engineer for acting quickly under pressure and skipping approvals
Remove the firewall from change control to avoid future delays
Define an expedited emergency path with retrospective review
Prohibit all emergency changes regardless of business impact
questions.explanation: Real emergencies need a defined fast path that still records, approves and reviews the change afterward. Rewarding bypass undermines control, removing the firewall from control increases risk, and banning emergency changes is unworkable.

questions.question: A critical patch for an actively exploited vulnerability has been released. The change advisory board next meets in three weeks. What is the BEST course of action?
options: Wait for the next scheduled meeting in three weeks regardless of the risk
Apply the patch to all systems immediately without any testing at all
Ignore the patch because the systems are protected behind a firewall
Use the emergency change process with quick testing and a rollback plan
questions.explanation: An actively exploited flaw justifies an expedited change with minimal but real testing and rollback readiness. Waiting weeks leaves exposure, skipping testing risks outages, and a firewall alone does not remove the vulnerability.

questions.question: A hospital's billing system has an RTO of four hours and an RPO of 30 minutes. Which backup and recovery approach BEST fits?
options: Weekly full backups to tape that are stored at an offsite location
Frequent replication or log shipping to a warm or hot site
Monthly backups combined with a cold site that must be built first
A reciprocal agreement with another hospital with no testing
questions.explanation: A 30-minute RPO needs near-continuous replication or very frequent backups, and a four-hour RTO needs a site that is largely ready. Weekly tape and a cold site would lose too much data and take too long, and an untested reciprocal arrangement is unreliable.

questions.question: The restore process must be as quick as possible while keeping daily backup windows short. Which scheme is BEST suited?
options: Full backup on Sunday with daily differential backups
Full backup on Sunday with daily incremental backups
Daily full backups only
Incremental backups with no full backup
questions.explanation: With differentials, a restore needs only the last full and the most recent differential, and the daily backup is smaller than a full. Incrementals give the shortest backup window but a longer restore, daily fulls have long windows, and incrementals with no full cannot restore at all.

questions.question: A company wants to test its disaster recovery plan without risk to production operations, but wants real recovery at the alternate site. Which test type should they use?
options: Full interruption test
Parallel test
Read-through test
Tabletop discussion
questions.explanation: A parallel test brings up the alternate site and processes data while production continues, so recovery is real and production is protected. A full interruption test shuts down production and is the riskiest. A read-through and a tabletop discussion do not exercise actual recovery.

questions.question: A data center needs fire suppression that minimizes the chance of accidental water discharge over expensive equipment. Which is the BEST choice?
options: A wet pipe sprinkler system
A dry pipe sprinkler with no detection
A pre-action system
Portable extinguishers only
questions.explanation: Pre-action systems need both a detection event and sprinkler head activation before water flows, reducing accidental discharge. Wet pipe holds water in pipes and can leak or discharge accidentally. Dry pipe alone lacks the added detection trigger, and portable extinguishers are not a suppression system.

questions.question: An employee in a sensitive role has never taken more than two days off in five years. Which control would BEST help detect possible fraud?
options: A longer password policy
A larger firewall
Additional antivirus software
A mandatory vacation policy
questions.explanation: Mandatory vacation puts another person in the role for a period so irregularities may surface, making it a detective control against fraud. Passwords, firewalls and antivirus do not address insider fraud concealed by continuous presence.

questions.question: Which two actions are appropriate during containment of a suspected malware incident on a server? (Choose two.)
options: Isolate the server from the network while preserving its memory and disk state for analysis
Document actions and timestamps in an incident log
Immediately wipe the server to remove the malware
Notify the attacker that they have been detected
Delete log files to reduce storage usage
questions.explanation: Containment stops spread while preserving evidence, and documentation supports later analysis and legal needs. Wiping immediately destroys evidence and root cause information, alerting the attacker may cause more damage, and deleting logs destroys the record.

questions.question: Which two statements about backup types are correct? (Choose two.)
options: A differential backup copies data changed since the last full backup
An incremental backup copies data changed since the last backup of any type
A differential backup needs every previous differential to restore
A full backup copies only changed files
Incremental backups give the fastest restore
questions.explanation: Differentials are relative to the last full and incrementals to the last backup of any type. A differential restore needs only the last full and the latest differential, a full backup copies everything, and incrementals are quickest to take but slowest to restore.

questions.question: Which two items should be reviewed in a post-incident lessons-learned session? (Choose two.)
options: What allowed the incident to occur and which controls failed or worked
Which detection and response steps were slow and what to change
Which employee to blame so they can be dismissed
How to conceal the incident from regulators
Whether to delete the incident log
questions.explanation: Lessons learned finds root cause and process improvements. Reviews are blameless, concealment from regulators may be illegal, and deleting the incident record removes evidence and organizational learning.

questions.question: Which two controls help ensure that backups will survive a ransomware attack? (Choose two.)
options: Immutable or offline copies that cannot be modified or deleted from the production network
Separate credentials for backup systems that production administrators cannot use
Storing backups on a share that every server can write to
Using the domain administrator account for backup jobs
Skipping restore tests to avoid overwriting data
questions.explanation: Ransomware seeks out and destroys reachable backups, so immutable or offline copies and separated credentials protect them. A widely writable share, a domain administrator account and untested backups all increase risk.

questions.question: An incident is an observable occurrence in a system, and every event should be treated as an incident.
questions.explanation: An event is any observable occurrence, and only those that actually or potentially violate policy or threaten confidentiality, integrity or availability are incidents. Triage separates the two.

questions.question: When collecting evidence from a live system, volatile data such as memory should be collected before disk contents.
questions.explanation: Memory and running state disappear on shutdown or change quickly, so the order of volatility puts them first.

questions.question: The maximum tolerable downtime must be shorter than the recovery time objective.
questions.explanation: The RTO must fit within the MTD, so the MTD is the larger limit. The RTO plus work recovery time must not exceed the MTD.

questions.question: RAID provides adequate protection against ransomware and accidental file deletion.
questions.explanation: RAID provides redundancy against disk failure but replicates deletions and encrypted data. Backups, especially offline or immutable ones, address those threats.

questions.question: A tabletop exercise is a discussion-based test that does not disrupt production systems.
questions.explanation: Tabletops walk participants through a scenario verbally, so they are inexpensive and safe, though they do not prove technical recovery works.

questions.question: Once litigation is reasonably anticipated, routine deletion schedules for potentially relevant records should be suspended through a legal hold.
questions.explanation: Destroying relevant data after a hold applies is spoliation and can lead to sanctions, so preservation duties override normal retention deletion.

questions.question: Application allow listing is generally stronger than block listing because it denies unknown software by default.
questions.explanation: Block lists must anticipate every bad program, while allow lists permit only approved software, so new malware is blocked without an update.

questions.question: A product team has a security review scheduled one week before release in each cycle and keeps finding design flaws that delay the launch. Which change BEST addresses the root cause?
options: Add another security review after release to catch what was missed
Hire more penetration testers for the final week before launch
Shift security left with requirements and design-stage threat modeling
Remove the final review so that releases are no longer delayed
questions.explanation: Flaws found late are costly to fix, so security requirements and threat modeling during design find them early. More reviews at the end or after release do not remove the cost of late discovery, and removing review just ships the flaws.

questions.question: A web page displays user comments exactly as submitted, and an attacker posts a comment containing a script that runs in other visitors' browsers. Which is the PRIMARY defense?
options: Longer passwords for the people who post comments
Contextual output encoding of comments
Using a stronger database encryption algorithm for stored comments
Increasing the session timeout for logged-in users
questions.explanation: This is stored cross-site scripting, and encoding data for the context where it is rendered makes the browser treat it as text, not script. Password length, database encryption and session timeout do not stop script injection.

questions.question: A developer builds a SQL query by joining strings with user input. Which control BEST prevents SQL injection?
options: Removing quotation marks and semicolons from all user input
Hiding detailed database error messages from the web page only
Encrypting the network connection between application and database
Parameterized queries with a least-privileged database account
questions.explanation: Parameterization separates code from data so input can never change the query structure, and least privilege limits damage if something slips through. Stripping characters is bypassable, hiding errors only reduces information leakage, and encrypting the connection protects traffic, not query logic.

questions.question: An attacker tricks a logged-in banking customer into clicking a link that silently submits a transfer request using the customer's active session. Which defense is MOST specific to this attack?
options: Anti-CSRF tokens validated on state-changing requests
Contextual output encoding of all user-supplied content on the page
Rate limiting on the login page to slow credential guessing
Disabling directory listing on the web server's document folders
questions.explanation: This is cross-site request forgery, which is stopped by unpredictable per-session tokens (plus SameSite cookies) that an attacker cannot supply. Output encoding addresses XSS, login rate limiting addresses guessing, and directory listing is unrelated.

questions.question: A program checks that a file is writable by the user and then, a moment later, opens it. An attacker swaps the file with a link to a protected file between the two steps. What flaw is this?
options: Buffer overflow
Time-of-check to time-of-use race condition
Cross-site scripting
Insecure deserialization
questions.explanation: The state changed between the check and its use, which is a TOCTOU race condition, fixed by making the check and use atomic. A buffer overflow writes beyond memory bounds, XSS runs script in a browser, and deserialization flaws involve untrusted serialized objects.

questions.question: An organization wants to find vulnerabilities in a running web application, including configuration and authentication problems, without access to source code. Which tool type fits?
options: Static application security testing
Software composition analysis
Dynamic application security testing
Peer code review
questions.explanation: Dynamic testing attacks the running application from outside and finds runtime and configuration issues. Static testing and peer review need source, and composition analysis inventories third-party components rather than probing behavior.

questions.question: A critical vulnerability is announced in a widely used open-source logging library. The security team needs to learn within hours which of the company's applications include it. What would have BEST prepared them?
options: A larger firewall budget for the perimeter and internal segments
A software bill of materials for every application
Annual penetration tests of the network and external perimeter
A policy banning all open-source software from every project
questions.explanation: An SBOM and composition analysis make it quick to identify where components are used. Firewalls and annual pen tests do not tell you which libraries are inside applications, and a ban on open source is unrealistic and does not remove existing use.

questions.question: A company is buying a commercial application that will process customer data. What should be done BEFORE signing the contract?
options: Assess the vendor's security practices and write security terms into the contract
Accept the vendor's claim that the product follows best practice and is secure
Plan to test security only after deployment into production, once users are on it
Rely on the product's popularity in the market as proof that it is secure
questions.explanation: Responsibility is not transferred with the purchase, so due diligence and contractual security requirements must come first. Taking claims on trust, testing only after production deployment and relying on popularity all leave unmanaged risk.

questions.question: An auditor finds database passwords hard-coded in application source code stored in a shared repository. What is the BEST remediation?
options: Make the repository private but leave the passwords in the code and its history
Obfuscate the passwords with a simple encoding so they are not readable at a glance
Add a comment asking developers not to share the code outside the team
Move secrets to a vault, rotate the exposed credentials and scan for secrets
questions.explanation: Exposed secrets must be treated as compromised and rotated, and a vault with runtime retrieval prevents recurrence. Restricting the repository leaves the secrets in history, encoding is not protection, and comments are not controls.

questions.question: A team runs a build pipeline that deploys to production automatically. An attacker who obtains a developer's pipeline token could ship malicious code. Which control BEST reduces this risk?
options: Protect pipeline credentials, require approvals and sign build artifacts
Make the pipeline run faster so deployments finish before an attacker can react
Store pipeline tokens in the source repository so the whole team can find them
Give every developer full administrator rights to the pipeline for flexibility
questions.explanation: The pipeline is part of the attack surface, so controlling credentials, requiring review and approvals, and verifying signed artifacts limit what a stolen token can achieve. Speed is irrelevant, and wide privileges or stored tokens increase risk.

questions.question: An Agile team delivers every two weeks. How should security BEST be integrated?
options: Perform one large security review after the final sprint of the project
Defer security to a separate project after the product has launched
Rely only on the operations team to protect the application once it is in production
Add security criteria to stories, with automated security tests each sprint
questions.explanation: Security must keep pace with iterations, through stories, acceptance criteria and automation. A single review at the end creates the same late discovery problem, and deferring or leaving it to operations leaves the code unprotected.

questions.question: The vendor of a business-critical application the company uses is a small firm. The buyer worries about what happens if the vendor goes out of business. Which arrangement addresses this concern?
options: A penetration test of the vendor's public website each year
Source code escrow with defined release conditions
A longer password policy for users of the application
A SOC 3 report from the vendor's auditor
questions.explanation: Escrow places the source with a neutral party and releases it to the customer under agreed conditions, such as bankruptcy. A website pen test, password policy and SOC 3 report do not protect continued maintenance of the software.

questions.question: A security architect wants to classify design-stage threats such as impersonation, data alteration and denial of service systematically. Which technique is BEST?
options: CVSS scoring
STRIDE threat modeling
Fuzzing
Regression testing
questions.explanation: STRIDE walks through a design looking for spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service and elevation of privilege. CVSS scores known vulnerabilities, fuzzing and regression testing operate on built software.

questions.question: Management asks how the organization can measure and improve its software security practices over time using a structured framework with prescriptive guidance. Which choice fits BEST?
options: OWASP Software Assurance Maturity Model (SAMM)
A SOC 2 report issued for a service provider
A one-time penetration test of the application
A change advisory board for production changes
questions.explanation: SAMM provides a prescriptive model to assess practices and plan improvements. A SOC 2 report is an attestation about a service, a pen test is a point-in-time technical test, and a change board manages changes.

questions.question: Which two actions are part of secure input handling in a web application? (Choose two.)
options: Validate input on the server using allow lists for expected format and length
Encode output for the context in which it is displayed
Rely on client-side JavaScript checks as the main protection
Block input only if it contains known attack strings
Accept any input and trust the database to reject bad data
questions.explanation: Server-side allow-list validation and contextual output encoding are the core practices. Client-side checks are bypassable, block lists miss variants, and trusting the database is a late and unreliable defense.

questions.question: Which two controls help protect the software supply chain? (Choose two.)
options: Verify signatures and provenance of dependencies and build artifacts
Pin dependency versions and monitor them for known vulnerabilities
Automatically pull the newest unverified package version at every build
Allow developers to publish builds from personal laptops
Disable logging in the build system
questions.explanation: Verification and pinned, monitored dependencies reduce the chance of tampered or vulnerable components. Pulling unverified newest versions, building on personal laptops and disabling logs all weaken integrity and visibility.

questions.question: Which two statements about SAST and DAST are correct? (Choose two.)
options: SAST analyzes code without running it and can point to the line of code involved
DAST tests a running application and can find runtime and configuration issues
DAST requires access to the application's source code
SAST can only be run after the application is deployed
SAST and DAST are identical and interchangeable
questions.explanation: SAST examines code statically early in development, and DAST probes a running build. DAST does not require source, SAST does not require deployment, and they find different issue types.

questions.question: A company is evaluating open-source components for a new product. Which two practices are appropriate? (Choose two.)
options: Maintain an inventory of components and versions, such as through an SBOM
Check licenses and known vulnerabilities before adopting a component
Assume widely used packages are always secure
Allow any developer to add dependencies with no review
Never update components after release
questions.explanation: Inventory and pre-adoption checks give control over both vulnerability and licensing risk. Popularity does not imply security, uncontrolled additions create unknown risk, and stale components accumulate vulnerabilities.

questions.question: Client-side input validation alone is sufficient to protect a web application from malformed or malicious input.
questions.explanation: Attackers can bypass the browser and send requests directly, so validation must be enforced on the server.

questions.question: Fixing a security defect during the design phase generally costs less than fixing it after release.
questions.explanation: Cost rises as a defect moves through the life cycle, which is the reason for shifting security left.

questions.question: A web application firewall is a replacement for fixing vulnerable code.
questions.explanation: A WAF is a compensating control that can provide virtual patching in the short term, but the underlying flaw should still be fixed.

questions.question: Code signing proves that the software contains no malicious code.
questions.explanation: Signing proves who published the code and that it was not changed afterwards. A signed program can still be malicious, particularly if a signing key is stolen.

questions.question: In the STRIDE model, repudiation refers to a user denying that they performed an action, countered by strong logging and non-repudiation controls.
questions.explanation: Repudiation threatens accountability, and logging, digital signatures and audit trails are the typical countermeasures.

questions.question: DevSecOps aims to automate security checks into the delivery pipeline instead of treating security as a separate gate at the end.
questions.explanation: DevSecOps integrates scanning, testing and policy checks into the pipeline so feedback comes early and releases stay fast.

lessons.title: Security Governance, Ethics, Compliance and Privacy
lessons.summary: How security is directed from the top, the ethics every CISSP is held to, and the legal and privacy duties that shape every decision.
lessons.reading:
Security governance answers a simple question: who decides what the organization protects, how much risk it will live with, and who is held accountable? The answer is senior management and the board. Governance is the direction and oversight they provide; management then turns that direction into plans, budgets and daily work. This is why the CISSP exam favors a top-down approach. A security program that starts with a technician's good idea but has no executive sponsor has no authority, no budget and no way to enforce anything. Whenever a scenario shows confusion, conflicting rules or cut funding, the best first move is nearly always to get senior-level direction and align security with the business goals.

Direction is written down in layers. A policy is a short, high-level, mandatory statement of management intent, such as "all laptops must be encrypted". Standards say precisely what is required, a baseline is the minimum configuration, procedures are the step-by-step instructions, and guidelines are optional advice. Reading from the top, each layer gets more specific; only guidelines are voluntary.

Underneath everything sit the core goals of security: confidentiality, integrity and availability, often called the CIA triad, plus authenticity and nonrepudiation. Access is controlled with AAA: authentication proves who you are, authorization decides what you may do, and accounting records what you did. Organizations choose a framework to organize their controls, such as NIST CSF (which in version 2.0 has six functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover), NIST SP 800-53, ISO/IEC 27001 (the standard an organization can be certified against), COBIT for IT governance, or SABSA for architecture.

Two ideas define professional responsibility. Due diligence is the research: understanding the risks and the options before acting. Due care is the action: doing what a reasonable person would do with that knowledge. An organization that studied a weakness and then did nothing has shown diligence but failed in due care, which is negligence. Ethics extends this duty to you personally. The ISC2 Code of Ethics has four canons, listed in order of precedence: protect society, the common good, necessary public trust and confidence, and the infrastructure; act honorably, honestly, justly, responsibly and legally; provide diligent and competent service to principals; and advance and protect the profession. When duties collide, the earlier canon wins.

Finally, security professionals work inside a legal environment. Intellectual property is protected through patents, copyrights, trademarks and trade secrets. Privacy laws attach to the data and the people it describes, not to where your servers sit: the EU's GDPR covers EU residents' data even when processed by a company elsewhere, and it requires breach notification to the regulator within 72 hours. In the United States, sector laws apply: HIPAA for health information, GLBA for financial institutions, SOX for public-company reporting, FERPA for student records and COPPA for children's data. PCI DSS, by contrast, is a contractual industry standard rather than a law.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to security governance? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Think of an organization as a ship. The board and executives are the owners who decide the destination and how much risk the voyage may take; that is governance. The captain and officers turn those orders into routes, rules and duty rosters; that is management. The crew follow procedures to keep the ship safe each day. If the crew make up their own rules with no instruction from the owners, the ship might still float, but nobody has the authority to enforce a safety drill or pay for lifeboats. Due diligence is the officer who studies the weather charts; due care is the officer who actually changes course when a storm is coming.
lessons.commonTraps: Mixing up due care (acting) and due diligence (researching) is the most common slip. Another is picking a technical fix when the scenario is really asking about management direction, such as policy approval and business alignment. Do not treat PCI DSS as a law, and do not assume GDPR depends on where your company is located. On ethics questions, remember the canon order: public safety outranks duty to the employer, but the right response is measured escalation, not publicity or silence.
lessons.scenario: A mid-sized insurer's regional offices each maintain their own password rules and incident procedures. After a minor breach, the board asks why a known weakness in the claims portal was documented a year earlier but never fixed. The CISO proposes a company-wide security policy approved by the CEO, a governance committee reporting to the board, and standards and procedures beneath the policy, and notes that the portal's EU customers bring GDPR obligations into scope.
lessons.onTheJob: Get executive sponsorship in writing before you build anything else; a policy signed by the CEO ends many arguments before they start. Translate every security request into business language: impact, regulatory exposure, revenue at risk. Keep a map of which laws apply to which data sets, reviewed with legal counsel, because the question is never just "are we secure?" but "are we compliant, and can we prove it?". Keep your own ethics file too: write down escalations and decisions, because they protect you as much as the organization.

lessons.title: Risk Management, Threat Modeling and Supply Chain Risk
lessons.summary: How to find, measure and treat risk, model threats before systems are built, and manage the risks that arrive through vendors.
lessons.reading:
Risk is the chance that something bad happens to something you value, and how bad it would be. Security professionals separate three ingredients. An asset is anything of value, a vulnerability is a weakness, and a threat is anything that could exploit it. Risk exists only when all three line up: a strong vault with no threats is not a risk, and a threat with nothing to exploit is not a risk either.
