Controls, also called safeguards or countermeasures, reduce risk by closing vulnerabilities or reducing threat impact. Because you can never reach zero, what remains after the controls is called residual risk, and the organization's appetite decides whether that remainder is acceptable.

Risk analysis comes in two styles. Qualitative analysis rates risks as high, medium or low using judgement and workshops; it is quick and easy to understand but subjective. Quantitative analysis puts numbers on it. The key formulas are single loss expectancy (SLE), which is asset value times exposure factor, and annualized rate of occurrence (ARO), the expected number of events per year. Multiplying them gives annualized loss expectancy (ALE). A control is worth buying when the ALE before it, minus the ALE after it, minus its yearly cost is positive. If a 400,000 dollar asset would lose a quarter of its value in a flood expected once every five years, the SLE is 100,000, the ARO is 0.2 and the ALE is 20,000 dollars.

Once risks are understood, management picks a treatment. You can mitigate by adding controls, transfer by using insurance or a contract, avoid by stopping the risky activity, or accept by knowingly living with it. Acceptance is always a business decision recorded by the risk owner; the security team recommends, it does not decide. Insurance transfers the financial cost but not the accountability, and ignoring a risk is not acceptance. For federal and many other organizations, the NIST Risk Management Framework gives a repeatable path: Prepare, Categorize, Select, Implement, Assess, Authorize, Monitor. The authorizing official is the person who accepts the remaining risk and approves the system to operate.

Threat modeling moves this thinking to the design stage, where fixes are cheapest. STRIDE asks, for each part of a design, whether an attacker could spoof an identity, tamper with data, repudiate an action, disclose information, deny service or elevate privilege. DREAD rates the seriousness of what you find. PASTA works through seven stages from business objectives to attack simulation, and attack trees draw the paths an attacker might take to a goal. The point is not to pick one favorite but to recognize each by its purpose.

Today a great deal of risk arrives through other organizations. Supply chain risk management covers counterfeit hardware, tampered software updates and a vendor's weak security. Good practice includes due diligence before choosing a supplier, security and breach-notification terms written into the contract, a right-to-audit clause, a software bill of materials for code you embed, signature checks on updates, and continuous monitoring of critical vendors. A requirement that is not in the contract cannot be enforced, so push security into the agreement before it is signed.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to risk management? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Imagine you own a house near a river. The house is the asset, the cracked foundation is the vulnerability, and the river flooding is the threat. You can mitigate by building a flood wall, transfer the cost by buying flood insurance, avoid the risk by selling the house, or accept it because the river has not flooded in fifty years. Even after the wall you still have some leftover risk, the residual risk. You would not spend more on the wall each year than the expected annual flood damage; that is the same logic as ALE. And if the builder you hired used cheap fake concrete, that is supply chain risk, which is why you check the supplier before the contract is signed.
lessons.commonTraps: Insurance is transfer, not elimination. Residual risk is not zero risk, and only management can accept it. Qualitative does not mean worse, only less precise. Do not confuse STRIDE (categories of threats) with DREAD (a scoring scheme). When a safeguard seems expensive, compare its annual cost to the reduction in ALE rather than to the asset's total value. And remember that the authorizing official, not the assessor or administrator, makes the risk-based decision to operate.
lessons.scenario: A company evaluates a 30,000 dollar annual web application firewall subscription. The current ALE for web application attacks is 90,000 dollars, and the vendor claims it would fall to 50,000. The CFO also asks whether buying cyber insurance means the project can be dropped, and procurement wants to buy cheaper network devices from an unvetted reseller to save money.
lessons.onTheJob: Keep a living risk register with an owner for each entry, and rerun the numbers whenever the business changes. Do not oversell quantitative precision: your inputs are estimates, so show ranges. Get risk acceptance signed by the person with the budget and authority, with an expiry date, so it is reviewed rather than forgotten. Insert security language into vendor contracts and master agreements early; negotiating after a vendor is entrenched rarely works.

lessons.title: Business Continuity, Disaster Recovery and Personnel Security
lessons.summary: Planning to keep the business running through disruption, recovery targets and sites, and controls that manage the people risk.
lessons.reading:
Business continuity planning keeps the critical functions of the organization running through a disruption, and disaster recovery planning is the part that restores IT systems, data and facilities afterwards. Neither starts with technology. They start with the business impact analysis, or BIA, which asks the business owners which processes matter most, what each depends on, and how much it would hurt to lose them over time. Only after the BIA do you choose recovery strategies; skipping it means guessing which systems to save first. Whenever a plan is described, the first priority is always the safety of people.

The BIA produces recovery targets that you must memorize. Maximum tolerable downtime (MTD, also called MAO) is the longest a business function can be unavailable before the organization's survival is threatened. The recovery time objective (RTO) is the time you aim to restore service, the recovery point objective (RPO) is how much data loss, measured in time, is acceptable, and the work recovery time (WRT) is the extra time to verify and reconfigure systems after restoration. RTO plus WRT must fit within the MTD, and a short RPO demands frequent backups or continuous replication. If a call center can be down for 8 hours but needs 6 hours to restore and 4 more to verify, the plan fails its own target.

Targets drive the choice of alternate processing site. A hot site is fully equipped and nearly in sync, recovering in minutes to hours at a high cost. A warm site has hardware and connectivity but needs data restored, recovering in hours to days. A cold site is just space and utilities, taking days to weeks, and mobile sites are relocatable trailers. Reciprocal agreements with another organization are cheap but hard to enforce. Pick the least expensive option that still meets the RTO; a hot site for a 36-hour requirement is waste, while a cold site for a 4-hour one is failure.

A plan that is never tested is a hope. Tests run from a read-through of the document, through a tabletop or structured walkthrough where participants talk through a scenario, a simulation, a parallel test that brings the recovery environment up alongside production, up to a full interruption test that actually shuts production down. Parallel tests are a popular balance because they prove recovery without risking operations. Plans must also be maintained when the business, staff or technology changes, and training ensures the right people know their roles.

People are both the greatest asset and a major source of risk, so personnel security matters. Hiring involves screening and background checks proportionate to the role, along with signed agreements such as NDAs. During employment, separation of duties splits critical tasks so collusion is needed for fraud, least privilege limits access, and job rotation and mandatory vacation expose irregularities that only the current holder of a role can hide. At departure the key is speed: disable accounts, retrieve badges and devices, and remind the employee of continuing obligations. For third parties, contracts and service level agreements must carry security duties, because outsourcing the work never outsources the accountability.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to business continuity? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: A family planning for a house fire does it in a sensible order. First they decide what matters (people, pets, photos, documents): that is the BIA. Then they set targets: everyone out within two minutes, and photos backed up to the cloud weekly. They choose a meeting spot across the street, a bit like picking a hot, warm or cold site, depending on how fast they need to resume normal life. Finally they practice the drill, starting with talking it through at the dinner table and later walking out of the house with the lights off. A plan nobody has practiced is just a piece of paper.
lessons.commonTraps: RPO is about data loss, not time to restore; RTO is the opposite. The BIA comes before the strategy, and business owners supply the impact figures. People's safety outranks equipment in every plan. Do not choose the hottest site by reflex: choose the cheapest that satisfies the RTO. A parallel test does not interrupt production, but a full interruption test does. And mandatory vacation is not a perk; it is a detective control for fraud.
lessons.scenario: A regional bank's online platform must be restored within 12 hours and can lose at most 5 minutes of transactions. The disaster recovery lead proposes a warm site with replication every 30 minutes. During the review, an auditor notes that the same administrator creates payees and approves payments and has not taken a vacation in four years.
lessons.onTheJob: Run the BIA with the people who own the processes, not just IT, and write the numbers down in a form executives will sign. Test at least annually and after major changes, and record what failed; the failures are the value. Keep call trees, vendor contacts and recovery credentials available offline. Fix separation of duties conflicts before an auditor or a fraudster finds them, and make offboarding a checklist owned jointly by HR, IT and security.

lessons.title: Asset Classification, Data Lifecycle and Privacy Controls
lessons.summary: Knowing what you have, deciding how sensitive it is, protecting it through its whole life and destroying it properly at the end.
lessons.reading:
Asset security begins with a plain idea: you cannot protect what you do not know you have. An accurate inventory of hardware, software, data and services, each with a named owner, is the foundation. Next comes classification, which assigns each information asset a sensitivity level, for example public, internal, confidential and restricted, or the equivalents used by governments. The level matters only because it drives handling rules: how the data is stored, who can see it, how it travels, how long it is kept and how it is destroyed. Classification is a business decision driven by value and legal duty, so the data owner decides, not the administrator.

Roles are a frequent exam topic. The data owner is the senior person accountable for the data, who sets its classification, retention and who may access it. The data custodian carries out the protections, such as backups, patching and access control operations, according to the owner's requirements. In privacy law the vocabulary shifts: the controller decides why and how personal data is processed, the processor works on the controller's behalf, and the data subject is the person the data describes.

Information has a lifecycle: it is created or collected, stored, used, shared, archived and finally destroyed. Controls must follow it through each stage. Data at rest is protected by encryption of disks, databases and backups. Data in transit is protected with TLS or IPsec. Data in use is the hardest, since it generally has to be decrypted in memory to be processed, which is why secure enclaves and strict access controls matter. Labeling helps people and tools handle each item correctly, and data loss prevention inspects content as it moves to block or flag unauthorized sharing of patterns such as card or national ID numbers.

Privacy-oriented techniques reduce what an attacker or an insider can do with data. Minimization means collecting and keeping only what is needed, and purpose limitation means using it only for the reason it was collected. Tokenization replaces a value, such as a card number, with a random surrogate while the real value stays in a protected vault. Masking hides part of a value for display or testing. Anonymization irreversibly removes the link to a person, so the result is no longer personal data, while pseudonymization uses a reversible code and the data stays regulated. Retention schedules say how long to keep each record, and a legal hold suspends deletion when litigation is reasonably anticipated.

The last stage is where many organizations fail. Deleting a file or quick-formatting a drive leaves recoverable data behind, called data remanence. NIST SP 800-88 describes three levels: clear (overwrite with standard commands), purge (stronger techniques such as cryptographic erase, which destroys the encryption key, or degaussing for magnetic media) and destroy (shred, disintegrate or incinerate). Degaussing does nothing to solid-state drives, so those need cryptographic erase, a verified secure-erase command or physical destruction. Choose the level by sensitivity and by whether the media leaves your control.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to asset security? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Think of a hospital's paper records. Each folder is labeled routine, sensitive or highly restricted, and the label tells staff where it may be stored, who may read it, and whether it can leave the building. The head physician (the owner) decides how sensitive each folder is; the records clerk (the custodian) files and locks them accordingly. Old folders are not just thrown in the bin: highly restricted ones go through a cross-cut shredder, and when a lawsuit is looming, a notice goes out to stop shredding anything related. Digital data deserves the same lifecycle thinking, from the moment the folder is created until the confetti is swept up.
lessons.commonTraps: The owner classifies the data; the custodian does not. Pseudonymized data is still personal data, but anonymized data is not. Degaussing works on magnetic media only, never on SSDs. Quick-formatting and deleting are not sanitization. A legal hold overrides a retention schedule. And masking is for display and testing, tokenization uses a vault, encryption uses a key: do not use the words interchangeably.
lessons.scenario: A hospital is replacing a rack of SSDs that held patient records and plans to sell the old drives to a reseller. A research group has asked for patient data to analyze outcomes, and the legal team has just told IT that a malpractice suit involving closed accounts is likely. The data steward asks which data can be released and how the old drives should be handled.
lessons.onTheJob: Start classification with the datasets that matter most, usually regulated data and crown jewels, rather than trying to label everything. Make labels visible to tools so DLP and cloud controls can act on them. Put sanitization requirements into contracts with disposal vendors and demand certificates of destruction. Review retention schedules with legal counsel each year, because keeping data forever is a liability, not a safety net.

lessons.title: Security Models, Secure Design Principles and Physical Security
lessons.summary: The formal models and design principles behind secure systems, the trust in hardware and cloud architectures, and the physical layer that underlies it all.
lessons.reading:
Security architecture is the discipline of building protection into a system from the start. The CISSP exam expects you to recognize a handful of design principles and apply them to scenarios. Least privilege gives every subject only the access it needs. Defense in depth layers independent controls so that one failure does not expose everything. Fail securely means that when a control breaks it defaults to a safe state. Secure defaults, separation of duties, economy of mechanism (keep it simple), complete mediation (check every access every time), open design (security should not depend on secrecy of the design) and privacy by design are the others you will see. Zero trust applies the same mindset to networks: no implicit trust because of location, and every request is verified using identity, device posture and context, as described in NIST SP 800-207.

Formal security models describe how a system can enforce a policy. Bell-LaPadula is about confidentiality: a subject cannot read up (simple security property) and cannot write down (star property), which stops secrets flowing to lower levels. Biba is the mirror image for integrity: no read down and no write up, which protects trusted data from contamination. Clark-Wilson is a practical commercial integrity model in which users change data only through approved transactions, with separation of duties and auditing. Brewer-Nash, the Chinese Wall model, changes a user's access dynamically to prevent conflicts of interest. A simple rule helps: if the scenario worries about disclosure, think Bell-LaPadula; about accuracy, think Biba or Clark-Wilson; about competing clients, think Brewer-Nash.

Models are implemented by trusted components. The reference monitor is the concept that every access between a subject and an object is mediated by a component that is always invoked, tamper-resistant and small enough to verify; the security kernel implements it, and the trusted computing base is everything that enforces security. Products can be evaluated under the Common Criteria and given an assurance level from EAL1 to EAL7, which describes how rigorously the product was tested, not how secure it is. Within an organization, certification is the technical evaluation, and accreditation or authorization is management's formal acceptance of the residual risk.

Special environments change the usual assumptions. Industrial control systems prioritize safety and availability and are often unpatchable, so they are segmented from corporate networks. In cloud services, the shared responsibility model means the provider secures the underlying infrastructure while the customer is always responsible for its data, identities and configuration.

Physical security protects everything above it. Mantraps prevent tailgating, lighting and design principles (Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design) shape behavior, and fire protection must match the hazard, with gaseous agents or preaction sprinklers in data centers to limit accidental water damage. Above all, human life safety comes first: exit doors fail open in a power loss, with compensating controls such as alarms and guards, even though that weakens access control.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to security architecture? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Picture designing a bank. You do not rely on one thick door; you build layers: street cameras, a locked lobby, a teller counter, a vault with a time lock, and a safe-deposit box inside (defense in depth). Each employee gets only the keys they need (least privilege), and two people must turn keys together for the vault (separation of duties). If the alarm panel loses power, the doors to the street must still open for anyone fleeing a fire (fail open for life safety), while the vault stays shut. The security models are like different house rules: one says secrets never leave the vault, another says nobody may alter the ledger except through the official forms.
lessons.commonTraps: Bell-LaPadula protects confidentiality, Biba protects integrity: do not swap them. A higher assurance level does not mean stronger features. Certification is technical; accreditation is management's risk decision. Zero trust is an approach, not a product to buy. Doors fail open for human safety even though that is less secure. In IaaS the customer, not the provider, secures the guest operating system.
lessons.scenario: A consulting firm is building a system for analysts who serve two competing banks. The architects choose a model that blocks an analyst from viewing the second bank's files after touching the first, require all changes through approved forms, and place the servers in a data center with a mantrap, preaction sprinklers and exit doors that unlock if power fails. A separate team wants to move administrators to a zero trust model.
lessons.onTheJob: When reviewing an architecture, ask what happens when each control fails, and whether any single person or component can defeat the whole design. Insist on threat modeling at design time. Treat vendor assurance claims as evidence to examine, not a guarantee. Walk the physical site yourself: tailgating, propped doors and unattended visitors are found by looking, not by reading policy.

lessons.title: Cryptography and Public Key Infrastructure
lessons.summary: Symmetric and asymmetric encryption, hashing, signatures, certificates and the key management that makes any of it trustworthy.
lessons.reading:
Cryptography transforms information so that only the right people can read it, trust it, or prove who sent it. The CISSP expects you to know the building blocks and, more importantly, which security goal each provides. Symmetric encryption uses one shared secret key, is fast and is used for bulk data; its weakness is distributing that key safely. Asymmetric encryption uses a mathematically linked pair: a public key anyone may have and a private key kept secret. It solves distribution and enables digital signatures, but it is slower. Real protocols combine both: asymmetric methods authenticate and exchange a session key, and a symmetric cipher such as AES protects the data.

AES is the current symmetric standard, with a 128-bit block and keys of 128, 192 or 256 bits; DES and 3DES are obsolete or deprecated. How a block cipher is used matters as much as the cipher: ECB mode encrypts identical blocks identically and reveals patterns, CBC chains blocks using an initialization vector, CTR turns the cipher into a stream, and GCM adds authentication so tampering is detected. Never reuse an IV or nonce with the same key. Among asymmetric algorithms, RSA relies on the difficulty of factoring, Diffie-Hellman lets two parties agree on a shared secret across an open channel (but needs authentication to stop a man in the middle), and elliptic curve cryptography gives equivalent strength with much shorter keys, which suits mobile and embedded devices.

A hash function turns data into a fixed-size digest and is one-way. It provides integrity checking, because any change alters the digest, but not authentication, because anyone can compute it. MD5 and SHA-1 are broken for collision resistance; SHA-2 and SHA-3 are current. Adding a secret key gives a message authentication code such as HMAC, which proves integrity and that the sender knew the key. A digital signature goes further: the sender encrypts the message hash with a private key, and anyone can verify it with the public key, giving integrity, authentication and nonrepudiation but not confidentiality. For passwords, use a slow, salted hash with a unique salt per password, which defeats rainbow tables.

A public key infrastructure provides trust in public keys. A certificate authority signs X.509 certificates that bind a public key to an identity; a registration authority validates requests; and revocation is published through certificate revocation lists or answered per certificate by OCSP. Trust flows from a root authority that must be kept offline and protected. If a private key is exposed, revoke the certificate and issue a new key pair; waiting for expiry leaves you open to impersonation.

Finally, key management is where cryptography usually fails. Keys must be generated with good randomness, protected in hardware security modules where the stakes are high, rotated, backed up or escrowed under split custody, and destroyed at the end. Dual control and split knowledge ensure that no single person holds a complete key. Looking ahead, quantum computers threaten RSA and elliptic curve algorithms, and NIST has standardized post-quantum algorithms, so organizations with long-lived secrets should inventory their cryptography and plan for agility.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to cryptography? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Symmetric encryption is like a padlocked box where sender and receiver both hold identical keys; fast, but how did you get the second key to your friend safely? Asymmetric encryption is like a public mailbox slot: anyone can drop a letter in (the public key), but only the owner has the key to open it (the private key). A digital signature works the other way round, like a wax seal only you could have made, which anyone can recognize. A certificate authority is the notary who confirms that this particular seal really belongs to this particular person, and the revocation list is the notary's list of seals that were stolen.
lessons.commonTraps: A hash does not authenticate and a MAC does not give nonrepudiation. A digital signature does not provide confidentiality. Key size is not block size. ECB is never the right mode. Diffie-Hellman without authentication is vulnerable to a man in the middle. After a private key compromise, revoke and reissue rather than waiting. Increasing RSA key length is not a defense against quantum computers.
lessons.scenario: A payment company needs to send signed, confidential files to a partner, protect its certificate authority's signing key, and fix a breach in which unsalted password hashes were cracked in hours. The architect also notes that the firm holds records that must stay secret for thirty years.
lessons.onTheJob: Use well-reviewed libraries and standard algorithms; never invent your own. Spend your effort on key lifecycle: where keys live, who can touch them, how they rotate, how you recover from compromise. Maintain a cryptographic inventory, since you cannot migrate to newer algorithms or respond to a weak-algorithm advisory without knowing where each one is used.

lessons.title: Secure Network Architecture: OSI, Segmentation and Perimeter Defenses
lessons.summary: The layered models that describe networks, the devices that operate at each layer, and the designs and tools that contain attackers.
lessons.reading:
Networks are described in layers so that each layer can be understood and secured separately. The OSI model has seven: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation and Application. The TCP/IP model compresses them into four: link, internet, transport and application. What matters for the exam is knowing where devices and attacks sit. Hubs and cables are Layer 1, switches work with MAC addresses at Layer 2, routers forward packets by IP address at Layer 3, and TCP and UDP port numbers live at Layer 4. ARP spoofing is a Layer 2 attack, IP spoofing is Layer 3, and a SYN flood is a Layer 4 attack. When a question names an attack, work out the layer first and the right control usually follows.

At Layer 4, TCP is connection-oriented and reliable. It opens a connection with the three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) and acknowledges data, while UDP is connectionless and lightweight. An attacker can send floods of SYN packets without finishing the handshake to exhaust the server's connection table, and mitigations include SYN cookies and rate limiting. Other denial-of-service attacks target bandwidth or application resources, and distributed versions come from thousands of sources, so blocking one address is pointless; the defense is capacity and upstream filtering through scrubbing services or a content delivery network.

Good network design assumes that something will eventually be compromised and tries to limit how far an attacker can move. Segmentation divides the network into zones by function or sensitivity, with firewalls or access lists controlling traffic between them. A screened subnet, often called a DMZ, sits between the internet and the internal network and holds public-facing servers so that a compromised web server does not give direct access to internal systems. VLANs create separate broadcast domains on switches, though they are not a security boundary without controls between them; attacks such as VLAN hopping are prevented by disabling unused ports and automatic trunking. Microsegmentation pushes the same idea down to individual workloads and is a core part of zero trust designs.

Firewalls come in several generations. Packet filters examine headers without tracking state. Stateful firewalls remember connections and permit return traffic for sessions the inside initiated. Application proxies and next-generation firewalls inspect traffic at Layer 7, adding application awareness, user identity and intrusion prevention, and a web application firewall protects HTTP applications from attacks such as injection and scripting. Place firewalls at every trust boundary, deny by default, and review rules regularly.

Detection complements prevention. An intrusion detection system monitors and alerts, usually from a copy of the traffic; an intrusion prevention system sits inline and can block. Signature-based detection recognizes known patterns and is accurate, but it misses a zero-day. Anomaly or behavior-based detection compares activity with a baseline and can spot the unknown, at the cost of false positives and tuning. In every design question, the strongest answer is the one that limits blast radius while keeping the business function working.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to network security? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Think of an office building. The OSI layers are like the postal system: the road (physical), the street addressing (data link), the city and zip code (network), the apartment number (transport) and finally the letter itself (application). A screened subnet is the lobby where visitors are met by reception without being allowed into the offices; internal zones are floors that need separate badges; microsegmentation puts a lock on each office. A firewall is the security desk checking who goes where, and an intrusion detection system is the camera room that notices someone behaving oddly, even if they have never been seen before.
lessons.commonTraps: Switches are Layer 2 and routers are Layer 3, and a Layer 3 switch routes. A VLAN alone is not a security boundary. Signature-based detection cannot catch a zero-day, and anomaly detection creates more false positives. An IPS is inline and an IDS is not. Distributed denial of service cannot be fixed by blocking one source. Putting public servers on the internal network, or directly on the internet, are both wrong answers when a screened subnet is available.
lessons.scenario: A retailer hosts its storefront on web servers that connect to an internal order database. After an attacker compromised a web server and scanned the internal network, the architect redesigns the network with a screened subnet, separate zones for payment systems and corporate users, and an inline IPS. A holiday flood of traffic from thousands of hosts later takes the site down, even though the firewall rules were correct.
lessons.onTheJob: Draw your network and every trust boundary before you change anything; most surprises come from paths nobody documented. Default-deny between zones, then open only what is justified and owned. Review firewall rule sets quarterly for stale entries. Tune detection tools with your own baselines, and plan for denial-of-service attacks with your provider before the first one arrives.

lessons.title: Secure Communications: Protocols, VPNs, Wireless and Remote Access
lessons.summary: The encrypted protocols, authentication services and wireless standards that protect data as it moves between people, sites and devices.
lessons.reading:
Data in transit crosses networks you do not control, so the first rule is to use the encrypted version of every protocol. Telnet becomes SSH, FTP becomes SFTP or FTPS, HTTP becomes HTTPS, LDAP becomes LDAPS, and older SNMP becomes SNMPv3. Transport Layer Security protects web traffic and many other applications; version 1.3 removed weak legacy options, requires forward secrecy so that a later key compromise does not expose past sessions, and shortens the handshake. If a scenario shows credentials crossing the network in clear text, the right answer is almost always the encrypted equivalent of the same service, not a stronger password or a different port.

IPsec protects traffic at the network layer. The Authentication Header provides integrity and authentication but not encryption, while Encapsulating Security Payload adds confidentiality. IKE negotiates the security associations. Transport mode protects the payload between two hosts, and tunnel mode encapsulates the whole original packet between gateways, which is the standard site-to-site VPN. Remote-access VPNs connect individual users, using IPsec or TLS-based designs. Split tunneling sends only some traffic through the tunnel, which saves bandwidth but lets internet traffic bypass corporate inspection and turns a compromised endpoint into a bridge. Zero trust network access improves on broad VPN access by granting per-application access after verifying identity and device posture, and SASE delivers such controls from the cloud.

Authentication for network access is usually centralized. IEEE 802.1X is port-based: a supplicant authenticates through an authenticator, such as a switch or access point, to an authentication server before any network access is granted, and network access control can also check device posture. The server is commonly RADIUS, which uses UDP, combines authentication and authorization and encrypts only the password. TACACS+ uses TCP, separates authentication, authorization and accounting and encrypts the whole payload, so it is favored for administering network devices.

Wireless networks broadcast to anyone nearby, so the standard matters. WEP is broken and must never be used. WPA2 uses AES with CCMP; Personal mode uses one shared passphrase, while Enterprise mode uses 802.1X with individual credentials, which gives accountability and lets you revoke one person at departure. WPA3 replaces the pre-shared key handshake with Simultaneous Authentication of Equals, which resists offline guessing and provides forward secrecy. Hiding the SSID and filtering by MAC address are not real controls. Threats include rogue access points attached to the network and evil twins that imitate a legitimate network; wireless intrusion prevention and mutual authentication address them.

Email and name resolution need their own protections. SPF lists which servers may send mail for a domain, DKIM signs messages, and DMARC tells receivers what to do when checks fail; together they fight domain spoofing but do not encrypt messages, which is the job of S/MIME or PGP. DNSSEC signs DNS records so resolvers can verify authenticity and integrity, while DNS over HTTPS or TLS encrypts queries for privacy but does not prove the data is genuine.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to secure communications? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Sending data over a network without encryption is like shouting your credit card number across a crowded room. TLS is stepping into a soundproof booth with the person you are talking to, after checking their ID. A VPN is a sealed armored tunnel between two buildings: outsiders can see that a tunnel exists, but not what travels through it. 802.1X is the guard at the building entrance asking each visitor for personal ID before opening any door, while the shared Wi-Fi passphrase is a single key given to everybody, and you cannot take it back from one person without changing the lock for everyone.
lessons.commonTraps: AH authenticates but does not encrypt; ESP can do both. DNSSEC gives authenticity and integrity, not confidentiality. SPF, DKIM and DMARC fight spoofing but do not encrypt mail. RADIUS encrypts only the password, TACACS+ the whole payload. Hidden SSIDs and MAC filters are weak. WPA2-Personal's shared key does not give per-user accountability. And split tunneling is a trade of visibility for bandwidth.
lessons.scenario: A professional services firm gives staff full-tunnel VPN access, and administrators log in to switches over Telnet. The office Wi-Fi uses one shared passphrase that a departed employee still knows. Customers have received phishing mail that appears to come from the firm's domain. The architect proposes SSH for management, 802.1X with individual credentials for Wi-Fi, per-application zero trust access for remote staff and SPF, DKIM and DMARC for mail.
lessons.onTheJob: Inventory every clear-text protocol on the network with a capture or flow tool; the list is usually longer than anyone believes. Move wireless to individual credentials early, since changing a shared passphrase is painful after the fact. Roll out DMARC in monitoring mode first, then quarantine, then reject, so you do not block legitimate mail. Keep management interfaces on a separate network and log every administrative session.

lessons.title: Authentication, Authorization and Access Control Models
lessons.summary: How systems decide who you are and what you may do: factors, biometrics, Kerberos and network access protocols, and the DAC, MAC, RBAC, ABAC family.
lessons.reading:
Every access decision starts with four ideas that are easy to blur together. Identification is claiming who you are, such as typing a username. Authentication is proving the claim. Authorization is the decision about what that proven identity may do. Accountability is being able to tie an action back to a person later through logs. The order matters on the exam: a system cannot authorize someone it has not authenticated, and accountability collapses if accounts are shared or the logs can be edited by the people being logged.

Authentication relies on factors. Something you know is a password or PIN, something you have is a token, smart card or phone, and something you are is a biometric such as a fingerprint. Multi-factor authentication means at least two different categories, so a password plus a security question is still one factor used twice. Biometrics bring their own vocabulary. The false acceptance rate (FAR) counts impostors let in, the false rejection rate (FRR) counts legitimate users turned away, and the crossover error rate (CER) is the point where the two are equal. A lower CER means a more accurate device, and it is the fair way to compare products because FAR and FRR can be traded against each other by adjusting sensitivity.

Kerberos is the network authentication protocol you must understand. A user proves identity once to the Authentication Service in the Key Distribution Center and receives a ticket-granting ticket. Whenever the user wants a service, that ticket is presented to the Ticket-Granting Service, which returns a service ticket for that one resource. The password never crosses the network after the first step, and the user does not keep typing it. For remote access, RADIUS provides authentication, authorization and accounting for network access with only the password encrypted, while TACACS+ separates the three functions and encrypts the entire session, which is why it suits administering routers and switches.

Once identity is established, an access control model decides authorization. In discretionary access control (DAC) the owner of a resource decides who else may use it, which is flexible but lets permissions drift. In mandatory access control (MAC) the system compares a clearance on the subject with a label on the object and owners cannot change the outcome, which fits environments where confidentiality is everything. Role-based access control (RBAC) attaches permissions to job roles and gives users roles, making administration and least privilege manageable. Attribute-based access control (ABAC) evaluates policy over attributes of the user, the data, the action and the environment, so it can say yes only if the device is healthy, the data is tagged for a project, and the request is within business hours.

Underneath all of the models are two principles. Least privilege gives people only what they need to do the job, and need-to-know limits access to the specific information required even for someone holding a clearance. Choose the model by asking where the decision should live. If it should live with the owner, think DAC. If it should be enforced by labels, think MAC. If it follows the job, think RBAC. If it depends on context that roles cannot capture, think ABAC.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to access control? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Picture entering a hospital. Telling the front desk your name is identification. Showing a photo ID and a badge that matches the list is authentication, and showing more than one kind of proof is multi-factor. What the badge opens afterward is authorization: a nurse can enter the ward but not the pharmacy vault. If the hospital lets each department head hand out keys, that is discretionary control. If the hospital stamps every document and badge with a security level and the doors enforce it, that is mandatory control. If doors open by job title, it is role-based, and if a door opens only for a doctor on duty, in the building, with a hospital-issued device, it is attribute-based.
commonTraps: A password and a security question are both knowledge factors, so the combination is not multi-factor authentication.
FAR counts impostors accepted (the security failure) and FRR counts legitimate users rejected (the usability failure); the CER, where they are equal, is the number to compare devices.
Rule-based and role-based sound alike but differ: rule-based applies global rules to everyone, role-based grants permissions by job function.
In Kerberos the ticket-granting service issues the service ticket; the authentication service only issues the ticket-granting ticket.
lessons.scenario: A regional bank wants administrators to manage its routers with per-command control and a full audit trail, while branch staff reach core banking applications only from compliant devices during working hours. The architect chooses TACACS+ for device administration, since it separates authorization and encrypts the entire session, and attribute-based policy for the applications, since device health and time of day cannot be expressed through static roles. Phishing-resistant security keys are issued for administrators.
lessons.onTheJob: Most real programs use several models together: roles for the bulk of access, attributes for sensitive exceptions, and mandatory labels only where regulation demands them. When asked to choose, pay attention to what is changing. A requirement that mentions device health, location or time is pointing at ABAC or risk-based access. Be wary of biometric projects that skip the privacy question, since a leaked fingerprint template cannot be reset like a password. Finally, remember that strong authentication is wasted if the account lifecycle is sloppy, so connect this lesson to provisioning and reviews.

lessons.title: Federation, Single Sign-On, Identity Lifecycle and Privileged Access
lessons.summary: SAML, OAuth and OpenID Connect, what single sign-on really buys you, joiner-mover-leaver, access reviews and managing privileged accounts.
lessons.reading:
Federation solves a simple problem: people at one organization need to use applications run by another, and nobody wants a second account to forget and abandon. In a federation an identity provider (IdP) authenticates the user and vouches for them to a service provider (SP), which trusts the IdP instead of holding a password. The cost is concentration: the IdP becomes critical infrastructure, so it needs high availability, strong multi-factor authentication and close monitoring.

Three standards dominate and are easy to mix up. SAML 2.0 is an XML-based standard that carries signed authentication and authorization assertions, mostly for browser single sign-on to enterprise and software-as-a-service applications. In a typical flow the user visits the SP, is redirected to the IdP, authenticates, and the IdP sends a signed assertion back through the browser. OAuth 2.0 is different in purpose: it is an authorization framework that lets an application obtain a scoped access token for another service, such as reading a calendar, without ever seeing the user's password. OpenID Connect sits on top of OAuth 2.0 and adds an ID token that says who authenticated, which is why modern sign-in with a corporate or social identity in web and mobile apps uses it. A useful memory hook is that OAuth authorizes, OpenID Connect authenticates, and SAML asserts identity for enterprise web single sign-on.

Single sign-on (SSO) is the user-facing benefit of federation: authenticate once and move between applications. It cuts password fatigue and helpdesk calls and gives one place to enforce policy, including conditional access that steps up to extra verification when risk rises. The trade-off is that a single stolen credential or session can open everything behind it, so SSO should be paired with multi-factor authentication and sensible session limits.

Identities have a lifecycle: joiner, mover, leaver. Accounts should be created from an authoritative source such as the human resources system, with approval from the data owner and only the access the role needs. Movers are the quiet danger. When someone changes jobs and keeps old access, privilege creep builds up until a person can both create and approve payments, a separation-of-duties failure. Leavers must have access removed promptly, and automation such as SCIM that is triggered by the HR event beats a manager remembering to send an email. Periodic access recertification asks managers and owners to confirm each entitlement, and reviews of privileged accounts should come more often than reviews of ordinary ones.

Privileged accounts deserve extra control because their misuse is catastrophic. Privileged access management vaults credentials, checks them out for a limited time, records the session, rotates the secret afterward and removes standing administrator rights, replacing shared passwords with named accountability. Just-in-time elevation grants rights only for a task and then removes them. When an exam question describes shared admin passwords, stale accounts or users with accumulated rights, the answer is almost always a lifecycle or privileged-access control, not a stronger password policy.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to federation? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Think of a passport and a border officer. Your home government (the identity provider) checks who you are once and issues a passport. A foreign country (the service provider) never sees your birth certificate; it trusts the passport because it trusts the issuer and can check the seal, which is the digital signature. A visa that lets you work only in certain jobs and only for a few weeks is like an OAuth token: limited scope, limited time. Joiners get a passport, movers get a new visa and must hand back the old one, and leavers have the passport cancelled.
commonTraps: OAuth 2.0 is authorization, not authentication; add OpenID Connect when the application must know who the user is.
Single sign-on reduces passwords but creates a concentrated target, so it demands strong MFA rather than relaxing it.
Stronger passwords do not fix orphaned accounts or privilege creep; those are lifecycle and review problems.
Outsourcing identity to a cloud provider does not outsource accountability for the policy and the data.
lessons.scenario: After an acquisition, a manufacturer has 60 cloud applications, three directories and frequent password resets. An audit also finds former contractors with active accounts and a shared administrator login documented on a wiki. The security architect federates the applications to a single identity provider that enforces MFA, links account removal to the human resources termination record using automated provisioning, schedules quarterly recertification for privileged groups and puts administrator credentials into a vault with session recording.
lessons.onTheJob: Start federation with the applications that cause the most helpdesk pain and the most risk, and plan for the identity provider outage before you move everything onto it, including break-glass accounts that are stored offline and monitored. The hardest part of lifecycle management is not technology but data: if the HR system is wrong about who is a contractor, automation will faithfully do the wrong thing. Make access reviews meaningful by showing reviewers who the person is and what the entitlement lets them do, since reviewers who see raw group names tend to approve everything.

lessons.title: Security Assessment, Testing and Audit
lessons.summary: Designing assessment strategies, choosing between scanning, penetration testing and audits, software testing, metrics and turning results into decisions.
lessons.reading:
Assessment and testing answer one question: do our controls actually work? A good strategy matches the activity to the question being asked and the audience that needs the answer. An assessment is a broad evaluation of controls against requirements. A test exercises a specific control, such as a vulnerability scan or a phishing simulation. An audit is a formal, evidence-based examination against a defined standard, and its value rests on independence. Internal audits are inexpensive and useful for readiness, external audits carry credibility with regulators and customers, and third-party audits examine suppliers.

When you rely on a service provider, you usually read their assurance reports rather than audit them yourself. SOC 1 covers controls relevant to financial reporting. SOC 2 covers the trust services criteria of security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality and privacy, and it is the report you normally want for a cloud or software-as-a-service vendor. SOC 3 is a short, public summary. Each of SOC 1 and SOC 2 comes in two types: Type I describes the design of controls at one date, while Type II also tests that they operated effectively over a period, so Type II gives much stronger assurance. Reading a report means checking the scope, the audit period, any exceptions and the controls the report expects customers to run themselves.

Technical testing has a ladder of intensity. A vulnerability assessment uses scanners to find and rank weaknesses without necessarily exploiting them, and credentialed scans, which log in to inspect patches and settings, are more accurate than unauthenticated ones. A penetration test goes further by exploiting weaknesses to show real impact and how findings chain together, which is why it needs written authorization and rules of engagement covering scope, timing, permitted techniques and emergency contacts. Testers may be black box (no knowledge), gray box (partial) or white box (full knowledge). Red teams emulate adversaries to test detection and response, and purple teaming has attackers and defenders collaborate so each technique improves a detection. Social engineering and wireless tests cover people and radio signals that scanners cannot see.

Software needs its own testing. Static analysis reads code, dynamic testing attacks the running application, and fuzzing feeds malformed input to find crashes. Misuse case and negative testing check that abuse fails, interface testing examines the trust boundaries where components meet, and regression testing makes sure fixes stay fixed. Coverage numbers tell you how much code ran, not whether the tests mattered.

Finally, results must become decisions. Raw findings are validated to weed out false positives, rated with business context (a CVSS score measures technical severity in general, not your risk), and reported with an executive summary and clear owners. Key performance indicators show how well a process runs, while key risk indicators warn of rising exposure. Continuous monitoring replaces occasional snapshots with an ongoing stream of evidence. The consistent exam answer is that a report must reach the people who can act on it, in language they can use.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to security testing? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Imagine checking the safety of a building. A vulnerability scan is a clipboard walk-through that lists every unlocked window and cracked lock. A penetration test hires a locksmith, with written permission, to actually get in and show how far they can go. An audit is a certified inspector, independent of the building manager, comparing the building to the fire code. A SOC 2 Type II report is like an inspector who watched how the sprinklers and alarms were maintained for a year rather than checking them once on a single afternoon.
commonTraps: A Type II report beats a Type I report because it tests operating effectiveness over time, not just design on one day.
A vulnerability scan finds weaknesses; only a penetration test demonstrates exploitation, and it needs written authorization first.
CVSS is generic severity, not your risk; prioritize by asset value, exposure and active exploitation.
An audit run by the people who operate the control lacks independence, however skilled they are.
lessons.scenario: A payments company must show customers that its controls work, and also wants to know whether an attacker could reach cardholder data. The security manager commissions an independent SOC 2 Type II examination for customer assurance, schedules monthly credentialed scans for patch accuracy, and signs rules of engagement with an external team for an annual gray box penetration test. The test report arrives with an executive summary ranking findings by business impact and names an owner and due date for each fix.
lessons.onTheJob: The most valuable habit is scoping. Many tests produce little value because nobody agreed what question they were answering. Before any penetration test, confirm the emergency stop contact and which production systems are fragile. Expect scanners to be noisy, so build a validation step into the process and track the false positive rate. When presenting to executives, show a trend and a decision, such as the percentage of critical systems patched within policy and what is needed to improve it, not a table of hosts. Keep evidence of control operation as you go, because audit season is miserable when you must reconstruct a year from memory.

lessons.title: Logging, Monitoring, Incident Response and Forensics
lessons.summary: Detecting attacks with logs, SIEM and endpoint tools, running the incident lifecycle, and preserving evidence so it can stand up in court.
lessons.reading:
You cannot respond to what you cannot see, so security operations begins with logging and monitoring. Logs from servers, applications, firewalls and identity systems should flow quickly to a central, protected store, where a security information and event management (SIEM) platform normalizes and correlates them and raises alerts. Three details are tested often. Clocks must be synchronized to a trusted source so events from different systems can be lined up. Logs must be protected from alteration, ideally by sending them off the system immediately and keeping administrators away from the record of their own actions. Retention must follow policy and law. Around the SIEM sit other tools: intrusion detection systems alert and intrusion prevention systems sit in line and block, endpoint detection and response watches behavior on devices and can isolate them, user and entity behavior analytics flags deviations from normal, and orchestration tools automate repetitive response steps. A SIEM that is not tuned either buries analysts in noise or misses the real attack.

An event is anything observable. An incident is an event or series of events that violates or threatens policy, so triage decides which events become incidents. The incident response lifecycle starts with preparation: the plan, the trained team with defined authority, tools, contacts and logging all have to exist before anything happens. Detection and analysis confirm what is going on and how serious it is. Containment limits spread, for example by isolating a host, while preserving evidence. Eradication removes the cause, such as malware and the access that let it in. Recovery restores systems, ideally from known-good sources, and monitors closely for reinfection. The final phase, post-incident review, asks what happened and what to change, without blame, and produces tracked improvements. The order matters: contain before eradicating, and eradicate before restoring.

Some incidents become investigations, and then evidence handling decides whether findings can be used. The forensic process runs from identification and preservation through collection, examination, analysis and reporting. Evidence is collected in order of volatility, from the most fragile to the most durable: memory and running processes first, then network state, then disk, then logs and archives. Pulling the plug before capturing memory throws away the best evidence. Investigators never analyze the original. They create a bit-for-bit image through a hardware write blocker and prove the copy is identical by comparing cryptographic hashes. Chain of custody records every person who handled the evidence, when and why, and a gap can make it inadmissible.

The type of case sets the rigor. Criminal matters need proof beyond reasonable doubt and the strictest handling, civil cases use the lower preponderance of evidence standard, and administrative or regulatory investigations follow internal policy or compliance rules. When litigation is reasonably expected, a legal hold suspends normal deletion so relevant records are preserved; destroying them afterwards is spoliation. Throughout, legal counsel and communications staff should be part of the team, and statements to outsiders should come from designated people.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to incident response? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Think of a hospital emergency department. Security cameras and monitors in every room are the logs, and the central nurses station watching them is the SIEM. Not every beep is an emergency: triage decides which events become incidents. Once there is one, the team stops the bleeding first (containment) before treating the underlying illness (eradication) and then helping the patient get back to normal life (recovery). Afterwards the doctors review the case to improve procedures. If a crime is involved, the clothes and samples are bagged, sealed and signed for at every handover, and the most perishable samples are taken first, which is chain of custody and order of volatility.
commonTraps: Rebuilding or powering off a compromised host immediately destroys volatile evidence; contain and preserve first unless life safety demands otherwise.
Lessons learned comes last and is not about blame, and preparation comes first and happens before any incident.
Hash values prove the copy matches the original; chain of custody proves who handled it. Evidence needs both.
An IDS only detects and alerts; an IPS sits in line and can block.
lessons.scenario: A SIEM alert shows an engineering workstation beaconing to a known malicious address at night. The analyst confirms the activity, opens an incident and the responder isolates the machine from the network without powering it off. Memory is captured first, then a write-blocked disk image is made and hashed, with each transfer recorded on a custody form. After the cause (a phishing link) is removed and credentials are reset, the host is rebuilt from a clean image. A blameless review leads to better email filtering and a new detection rule.
lessons.onTheJob: Practice the plan before you need it: tabletop exercises reveal missing phone numbers, unclear authority and the fact that nobody can remember who talks to the press. Keep an offline copy of the plan and contact list, since the systems you would read it on may be the ones affected. Tune detections continuously, retire rules that never fire usefully, and measure time to detect and time to contain. Involve legal counsel early, particularly where regulators or customers must be notified within deadlines, and write incident notes as if they will be read in court.

lessons.title: Resilience, Recovery, Change and Physical Operations
lessons.summary: Recovery objectives, backups and alternate sites, testing the plan, configuration, patch and change management, and physical and personnel safety in daily operations.
lessons.reading:
Resilience planning starts with the business, not the technology. A business impact analysis identifies the critical processes and sets the numbers that drive everything else. The maximum tolerable downtime (MTD, also called maximum allowable outage) is how long a process can be down before the organization is in serious trouble. The recovery time objective (RTO) is the target to restore the service, and it plus the work recovery time needed to verify data and resume work must fit inside the MTD. The recovery point objective (RPO) is how much data you can afford to lose, measured in time, and it sets how often you must back up or replicate. A business continuity plan keeps critical business functions running through any disruption. A disaster recovery plan is the technology-focused part that restores systems and data.

Backups implement the RPO. A full backup copies everything. An incremental backup copies what changed since the last backup of any type, so it is quick to take but a restore needs the last full plus every incremental since. A differential copies what changed since the last full, so it grows each day but a restore needs only the last full and the latest differential. Follow the 3-2-1 idea of three copies, two media types and one offsite, and make at least one copy immutable or offline, because ransomware hunts for reachable backups. RAID and clustering are redundancy for availability, not backup, since they faithfully copy deletions and encryption. Above all, test restores; a backup that has never been restored is only a hope.

The RTO selects the alternate site. A hot site is fully equipped with current data and can take over in minutes to hours. A warm site has hardware and connectivity but needs data and configuration brought in. A cold site offers only space, power and cooling, and is cheap but slow. Plans are proven through a ladder of tests: a read-through of the document, a tabletop or walkthrough discussion, a simulation, a parallel test that recovers at the alternate site while production keeps running, and a full interruption test that actually switches production, which carries the most risk.

Day-to-day operations keep that environment predictable. Configuration management defines secure baselines, tracks every item in an inventory and detects drift. Patch management identifies, tests, deploys and verifies updates, with a fast path for actively exploited flaws. Change management routes alterations through request, risk review, approval, implementation, verification and documentation, often with a change advisory board, and defines an emergency path with review after the fact. Security belongs in this process because unreviewed changes are how outages and exposures arrive.

Physical and personnel matters complete the picture. Defense in depth places layers from the perimeter to the room to the rack. Pre-action sprinklers are the common choice for data centers because water needs two triggers, and gas agents protect without water damage but must be safe for people. Life safety comes first: evacuation, duress codes, travel briefings and workplace violence prevention protect people before property.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to disaster recovery? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Consider a restaurant. The business impact analysis says the kitchen can be closed for about four hours on a Saturday night before regulars are lost, which is the maximum tolerable downtime. The recovery time objective is how fast the owner promises to reopen, and the recovery point objective is how many orders written down since the last time they were safely copied can be lost. A hot site is a second kitchen, fully stocked and running next door. A warm site is an empty kitchen with ovens installed. A cold site is a rented room with a power outlet. Change management is the rule that nobody rearranges the kitchen during service without telling the head chef.
commonTraps: The RTO plus work recovery time must fit within the MTD; the MTD is the outer limit, not the target.
Incremental is quickest to back up but slowest to restore; differential is larger to back up but faster to restore.
RAID and clustering protect availability from hardware failure; they do not protect against deletion, corruption or ransomware.
A parallel test does not interrupt production; a full interruption test does and is the riskiest.
lessons.scenario: A hospital billing system has an MTD of eight hours, an RTO of four and an RPO of 30 minutes. The team replicates the database to a warm site every ten minutes, keeps nightly backups with an offline copy, and rehearses a parallel failover twice a year. A critical remote-code-execution patch is released on a Tuesday, so the team uses the emergency change path: a rapid test on a staging replica, deployment with a rollback plan, and a retrospective review at the next advisory board meeting.
lessons.onTheJob: Most recovery plans fail on dependencies nobody wrote down: the directory service, the licensing server, the person who knows a password. Map them during the business impact analysis, and rehearse with the staff who will actually be on call, not the people who wrote the plan. Treat backup restoration time as a measured number, because data volumes grow and yesterday's RTO silently becomes unachievable. Keep your change calendar visible to security so that detections of unexpected change have context, and make the emergency path real but costly enough that it is not used for convenience.

lessons.title: Secure Software Development and Acquired Software
lessons.summary: Building security into development life cycles and DevSecOps, common coding flaws and defenses, application security testing, and trusting software you did not write.
lessons.reading:
A software development life cycle is the sequence of requirements, design, development, testing, deployment and maintenance through which software passes, and the central idea of secure development is that security belongs in every phase rather than at the end. Security requirements are written with the functional ones, threat modeling examines the design before code exists, developers follow secure coding standards, testing includes security tests, deployment is hardened, and maintenance includes patching and eventually secure retirement. The reason is cost: a design flaw found in review is cheap to fix, and the same flaw found after release can be ruinous. Moving security earlier is called shifting left.

Methodologies change how this is done but not whether. Waterfall completes phases in order with heavy documentation. Agile works in short iterations, so security has to appear as stories, acceptance criteria and automated tests inside each sprint. DevOps joins development and operations through automation, and DevSecOps adds security checks, policy and testing into the same pipeline so feedback is fast. The pipeline itself becomes a target, because whoever controls it controls what ships; protect its credentials, require review and approval, and sign and verify build artifacts.

Threat modeling with STRIDE asks, for each component and data flow, about spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service and elevation of privilege. Coding flaws are the other half. SQL injection, in which input alters a database query, is stopped by parameterized queries and least-privileged database accounts. Cross-site scripting, in which a victim's browser runs attacker script, is stopped by output encoding appropriate to the context, supported by a content security policy. Cross-site request forgery, in which a logged-in browser is tricked into sending a request, is stopped by anti-forgery tokens and SameSite cookies. Buffer overflows, caused by writing past the end of a buffer, are reduced by bounds checking and memory-safe languages. A recurring principle is to validate input on the server using allow lists and to encode output for where it lands.

Testing complements design. Static analysis reads source code early and points to the line at fault. Dynamic testing attacks the running application and finds configuration and runtime problems. Interactive testing uses instrumentation inside the app during tests. Software composition analysis inventories open-source components and flags known vulnerable versions, and a software bill of materials is the formal list that lets you answer quickly whether a newly announced flaw affects you.

Most software today is partly or wholly written by someone else, and responsibility does not transfer with the purchase. Assess commercial, open-source and software-as-a-service products for the vendor's development practices, testing evidence, patch commitments, licensing and data handling before you adopt them. Protect the supply chain by verifying signatures and provenance, pinning and monitoring dependencies, and controlling who can publish builds. Code signing proves who published code and that it was unchanged, but not that it is safe.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to secure development? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Think of building a house. An architect who thinks about burglars while drawing the plans can put windows in sensible places for almost nothing. A building inspector who notices the problem after the walls are up has to tear things out. That is shifting left. Using pre-made components such as windows or wiring means trusting the manufacturer, so you check certificates and keep a list of what went in, which is the bill of materials, so that a recall notice can be matched to your house in minutes.
commonTraps: Security reviews only at the end of a cycle find flaws when they are most expensive to fix; the right answer shifts security earlier.
Parameterized queries beat escaping or blocklisting for SQL injection, and contextual output encoding is the primary defense for cross-site scripting.
A web application firewall is a compensating control, not a substitute for fixing the vulnerable code.
Code signing proves origin and integrity, not that the code is free of malware or flaws.
lessons.scenario: A software company ships every two weeks. Its security team adds a threat-modeling checklist to design reviews and writes security acceptance criteria into stories. The pipeline runs static analysis and secret scanning on every commit, composition analysis on dependencies, and dynamic scans against a test environment before release, then signs the artifact. When a flaw in a popular open-source library is announced, the generated software bill of materials shows within minutes which three products are affected.
lessons.onTheJob: Tools only help if developers trust them. Start with a small set of high-confidence rules so that findings are real, route results into the tracker developers already use, and measure the time to fix instead of the count of findings. Secure coding guidance works best as short, concrete patterns in the languages your teams use. For acquired software, put security requirements in the contract and request the vendor's testing evidence before you sign; after signing you have much less leverage. And treat the build system as production, with its own access control, logging and monitoring.

cheatSheet.heading: Domain 1: Governance, ethics and law
points: Security serves the business: governance is set by senior management (top-down), policies are mandatory, standards are mandatory and specific, procedures are step-by-step, guidelines are optional, baselines are minimums.
Due diligence = research and understand the risk; due care = act on it. Failing due care is negligence.

ISC2 Code of Ethics canons in order: protect society, the common good, public trust and the infrastructure; act honorably, honestly, justly, responsibly and legally; provide diligent and competent service to principals; advance and protect the profession.

GDPR follows the data subject (EU residents) wherever the processor is, with regulator notice within 72 hours; HIPAA = health, GLBA = financial, SOX = public-company reporting, FERPA = students, COPPA = children under 13; PCI DSS is contractual, not a law.

Intellectual property: patent (invention), copyright (expression), trademark (brand), trade secret (kept confidential). Evidence: chain of custody, hash the image, work on copies; civil standard is preponderance, criminal is beyond a reasonable doubt.

cheatSheet.heading: Risk management formulas and treatment
points: Risk = threat x vulnerability x impact. SLE = asset value x exposure factor; ALE = SLE x ARO. Safeguard value = ALE before - ALE after - annual cost of safeguard.
Treatments: mitigate, transfer (insurance, contract), avoid, accept. Only the risk owner or senior management accepts risk; insurance never transfers accountability.
NIST RMF (SP 800-37 Rev. 2): Prepare, Categorize, Select, Implement, Assess, Authorize, Monitor. The authorizing official accepts residual risk.
NIST CSF 2.0 functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover.
Threat modeling: STRIDE (categories), DREAD (scoring), PASTA (seven-stage risk-centric), attack trees. Do it early in design.
Supply chain risk: vendor due diligence, security terms and right to audit in the contract, SBOM, signed updates, authorized sources only.

cheatSheet.heading: Continuity, recovery and personnel
points: BIA comes first and is answered by business owners. It sets MTD (outer limit), RTO (time to restore), RPO (tolerable data loss) and WRT (verification); RTO + WRT must fit inside MTD.
Sites: hot (minutes to hours, costly), warm (hours to days), cold (days to weeks), mobile, reciprocal (hard to enforce). Pick the cheapest that meets the RTO.
Tests from least to most disruptive: read-through, tabletop, simulation, parallel, full interruption. Parallel proves recovery without stopping production.
People safety is always the first priority in any plan.
Personnel controls: screening, NDAs, separation of duties, least privilege, job rotation, mandatory vacation, fast and complete offboarding. Outsourcing never outsources accountability.

cheatSheet.heading: Domain 2: Asset security
points: Data owner classifies and decides access and retention; custodian implements protections; steward looks after quality. Controller decides purposes, processor acts for the controller, data subject is the person.
Lifecycle: create, store, use, share, archive, destroy. States: at rest, in transit, in use (hardest to protect).
Sanitization (NIST SP 800-88): clear, purge (cryptographic erase, degaussing for magnetic), destroy. Degaussing does not work on SSDs; deleting and quick-formatting leave data remanence.
Tokenization = vault-based surrogate; masking = hide part for display; anonymization is irreversible, pseudonymization is reversible and still personal data.
Minimization and purpose limitation reduce privacy risk. A legal hold overrides retention schedules. End-of-support systems need isolation, compensating controls and a documented acceptance.

cheatSheet.heading: Domain 3: Architecture, models and physical security
points: Design principles: least privilege, defense in depth, fail securely, secure defaults, separation of duties, simplicity, complete mediation, open design, privacy by design, zero trust (never trust, always verify).

Models: Bell-LaPadula = confidentiality (no read up, no write down); Biba = integrity (no read down, no write up); Clark-Wilson = well-formed transactions and separation of duties; Brewer-Nash = conflict of interest.

Reference monitor mediates all access; TCB is everything enforcing security; Common Criteria EAL1 to EAL7 measures evaluation rigor, not strength; certification is technical, accreditation is management acceptance of residual risk.

Shared responsibility: the customer always owns data, identities and configuration. ICS and OT put availability and safety first and need segmentation; IoT needs unique credentials and network controls.
Physical: layered defenses, mantrap stops tailgating, preaction sprinklers or gaseous agents in data centers, exits fail open for life safety.

cheatSheet.heading: Cryptography and PKI
points: Symmetric (AES, fast, one shared key) for bulk data; asymmetric (RSA, ECC, Diffie-Hellman) for key exchange and signatures. Number of keys: symmetric n(n-1)/2, asymmetric 2n.
AES: 128-bit block, 128, 192 or 256-bit keys. DES and 3DES are obsolete or deprecated. ECB reveals patterns; prefer authenticated modes such as GCM; never reuse an IV or nonce.

Hash = integrity only; HMAC = integrity and authenticity with a shared key; digital signature (sender private key) = integrity, authentication and nonrepudiation but not confidentiality. For confidentiality encrypt with the recipient public key.
Passwords: slow, salted hashes with a unique salt per password; salts defeat rainbow tables.
PKI: CA signs X.509 certificates, RA verifies identity, CRL or OCSP for revocation, keep the root offline. If a private key is exposed, revoke and reissue.
Key management: HSM, dual control, split knowledge, rotation, escrow under split custody. NIST has standardized post-quantum algorithms (ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA); plan crypto agility.

cheatSheet.heading: Domain 4: Network security
points: OSI: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application. Switch = Layer 2 (MAC), router = Layer 3 (IP), TCP/UDP = Layer 4. ARP spoofing is L2, SYN flood is L4.
Use the encrypted twin: SSH not Telnet, HTTPS not HTTP, SFTP or FTPS not FTP, LDAPS not LDAP, SNMPv3. TLS 1.3 requires forward secrecy; SSL is deprecated.
IPsec: AH = integrity and authentication only; ESP = adds confidentiality; tunnel mode between gateways, transport mode host to host; IKE negotiates keys.
Screened subnet (DMZ) for public servers; segment and microsegment to limit lateral movement; a VLAN alone is not a security boundary. Firewalls: packet filter, stateful, proxy, NGFW, WAF (HTTP).
IDS alerts, IPS blocks inline. Signature = known attacks; anomaly = unknown but false positives. DDoS is fought upstream (scrubbing, CDN), not by blocking one address.

RADIUS (UDP, password only encrypted) vs. TACACS+ (TCP, full payload encrypted, device admin); 802.1X for port-based authentication. WPA3 (SAE) > WPA2 > never WEP; Enterprise for accountability. SPF, DKIM and DMARC stop domain spoofing; DNSSEC gives DNS authenticity, DoH and DoT give privacy.

cheatSheet.heading: Exam format and domain weights
