points: Eight domains: Security and Risk Management 16%, Asset Security 10%, Security Architecture and Engineering 13%, Communication and Network Security 13%, Identity and Access Management 13%, Security Assessment and Testing 12%, Security Operations 13%, Software Development Security 10%. This is the outline in effect since April 15, 2024.
Experience: five years of paid work in two or more domains, with one year waivable by a degree or an approved credential. Without the experience you can pass the exam and become an Associate of ISC2.
The Code of Ethics is examinable and must be followed in order of canons.

cheatSheet.heading: Exam-day strategy
points: Format: a computerized adaptive test with 100 to 150 items in up to 3 hours; the exam ends when the engine is confident of your result, at 150 items or when time expires. Scoring is scaled 0 to 1000 with 700 to pass; the scale is not a percentage correct.

Items include multiple choice and advanced innovative items such as drag-and-drop and hotspot. In the adaptive format you cannot go back to a previous question, so answer each one deliberately and never leave one blank.

Think like a risk advisor or manager, not a technician. The best answer is usually the one that aligns with business objectives, involves the right decision maker and addresses root cause, not the most technical or most expensive fix.

Read the last line first to see the ask: FIRST, BEST, MOST or LEAST. For FIRST, look for assessment, understanding or approval before action; for BEST, several options may work, so choose the one that fits the stated constraints and is proportionate.

Eliminate technically correct but wrong-timing options (a tool when the problem is policy, a fix before a risk assessment, a hot site before a BIA). Human life and safety come first, then legal and ethical duties, then business value.

Never choose an answer that is unethical, illegal or hides information from management. Watch for absolutes such as always and never, and for the accountability trap: responsibility cannot be transferred, only tasks and financial impact.

Pace yourself at about a minute and a half per item on average, do not dwell on a single hard question because later ones will not be easier, and trust your first reasoned answer unless you spot a specific detail you misread.

cheatSheet.heading: IAM essentials (Domain 5)
points: Identification claims, authentication proves, authorization permits, accountability records. Authenticate before you authorize.
Factors: know, have, are. Multi-factor needs two different categories; a password plus a security question is single-factor.
Biometrics: FAR is impostors accepted (Type II), FRR is legitimate users rejected (Type I), and the lower CER is the more accurate device.
Most phishing-resistant: FIDO2/WebAuthn. TOTP and SMS codes can be relayed by a phishing proxy. NIST SP 800-63B favors length and breached-password checks, and no forced periodic rotation.
Least privilege, need-to-know, separation of duties (split the task), dual control (two act together), split knowledge (each knows part).

cheatSheet.heading: Access control models and protocols
points: DAC: owner decides. MAC: labels and clearances enforced by the system. RBAC: permissions by job role. Rule-based: global rules such as ACLs. ABAC: policy over subject, object, action and environment attributes.

Kerberos: authentication service gives a ticket-granting ticket, the ticket-granting service gives a service ticket; needs synchronized clocks; the key distribution center is a single point of failure.
RADIUS: UDP, encrypts only the password, network access. TACACS+: TCP, encrypts the whole payload, separates authentication, authorization and accounting, device administration.
Risk-based or context-aware access adapts authentication to signals such as location, device posture and behavior (conditional access, zero trust).

cheatSheet.heading: Federation, lifecycle and privileged access
points: SAML 2.0: XML assertions for browser enterprise SSO. OAuth 2.0: delegated authorization with scoped tokens. OpenID Connect: authentication layer (ID token) on OAuth. OAuth authorizes, OIDC authenticates.
The identity provider authenticates and signs; the service provider trusts the assertion. SSO reduces passwords but concentrates risk, so pair it with strong MFA.
Joiner, mover, leaver: leavers and movers are where audits find orphaned accounts and privilege creep. Automate from the HR record (SCIM) and run periodic recertification.
PAM: vault, check-out, rotate, record sessions, remove standing rights, just-in-time elevation. Shared admin passwords with no attribution are the classic wrong state.

cheatSheet.heading: Assessment, testing and audit (Domain 6)
points: Assessment is broad, test is specific, audit is formal and independent. External audits carry the most credibility with outsiders; internal audits suit readiness.

SOC 1: financial reporting. SOC 2: security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, privacy (restricted use). SOC 3: public summary. Type II tests operation over time; Type I is design at one date.

Vulnerability scan finds and ranks; penetration test exploits to show impact and needs written authorization and rules of engagement. Black, gray and white box describe tester knowledge; credentialed scans are more accurate.
CVSS is generic technical severity, not your risk. Validate findings for false positives; false negatives are the dangerous ones.

Software testing: static (code), dynamic (running), interactive, fuzzing, misuse cases, interface testing, regression. KPIs measure performance, KRIs signal rising risk. Report to people who can act, with an executive summary.

cheatSheet.heading: Operations: monitoring, incidents and forensics (Domain 7)
points: Centralize and protect logs, synchronize time (NTP), set retention by policy and law, and separate log access from the people being logged. A SIEM must be tuned.

Event is any occurrence; incident violates or threatens policy. Lifecycle: preparation, detection and analysis, containment, eradication, recovery, post-incident review (blameless, with tracked actions).
Contain, then eradicate, then restore. Restore from known-good sources and monitor for reinfection. Preparation happens before the incident.
Forensics: preserve, image with a write blocker, verify hashes, document chain of custody, collect in order of volatility (memory, network state, disk, logs, archives). Never analyze the original.
Standard of proof: criminal beyond reasonable doubt, civil preponderance. Legal hold suspends deletion when litigation is anticipated.

cheatSheet.heading: Recovery, change and software security (Domains 7 and 8)
points: RTO plus work recovery time must fit within MTD; RPO sets backup frequency. Hot site fastest and costliest, warm in between, cold cheapest and slowest.
Full copies all; incremental is smallest to take and slowest to restore; differential needs the last full plus the latest differential. 3-2-1 with an immutable or offline copy. RAID is not a backup.

DR tests from least to most disruptive: read-through, tabletop, simulation, parallel, full interruption. Pre-action sprinklers suit data centers. Emergency changes get an expedited path with review afterward.
Shift security left; Agile needs security stories and automated tests; DevSecOps puts checks in the pipeline and protects the pipeline itself. STRIDE is the design-stage threat model.

SQL injection: parameterized queries. XSS: output encoding. CSRF: anti-forgery tokens and SameSite cookies. Overflows: bounds checks and memory-safe languages. Race conditions: atomic check and use. Validate input on the server with allow lists.

SAST reads code early, DAST attacks the running app, SCA and SBOM track components. A WAF is compensating, and code signing proves origin, not safety. Assess acquired software before buying; escrow protects against vendor failure.

madlibs.scenario: A server holding customer records is worth 200,000 dollars, and a fire would destroy half of it, so the single loss expectancy is {b1}. If such a fire is expected once every ten years, the annualized loss expectancy is {b2}. Management can reduce the financial impact by buying an insurance policy, which is risk {b3}.

options: 10,000 dollars
100,000 dollars
200,000 dollars
10,000 dollars
100,000 dollars
20,000 dollars
avoidance
acceptance
transfer

madlibs.explanation: SLE = asset value x exposure factor = 200,000 x 0.5 = 100,000. ARO is 1 in 10 years = 0.1, so ALE = 100,000 x 0.1 = 10,000 dollars. Insurance shifts the financial loss to another party, which is transfer; it does not remove the threat or the accountability.

madlibs.scenario: A retailer's business impact analysis states that its payment system can lose at most 10 minutes of transactions; this tolerance is the {b1}. It also says the system must be back in service within 4 hours, which is the {b2}. The longest the business could be without the system before its survival is threatened is the {b3}.

options: recovery point objective
recovery time objective
maximum tolerable downtime
recovery point objective
work recovery time
recovery time objective
recovery point objective
maximum tolerable downtime
recovery time objective

madlibs.explanation: RPO measures acceptable data loss in time and drives backup and replication frequency. RTO is the target time to restore service. MTD is the outer limit of outage the business can survive, and RTO plus work recovery time must fit inside it.

madlibs.scenario: Before retiring a set of hard drives that held confidential data, the team decides to expose them to a strong magnetic field, which is called {b1}. This works on magnetic media but not on {b2}, which instead need cryptographic erase or physical destruction. Of the three NIST sanitization levels, shredding the media is {b3}.

options: tokenization
data masking
degaussing
spinning hard drives
solid-state drives
magnetic tapes
destroy
clear
purge

madlibs.explanation: Degaussing erases magnetic media by disrupting the magnetic domains and has no effect on flash memory. Under NIST SP 800-88 the levels are clear, purge and destroy; physical shredding or disintegration is destroy.

madlibs.scenario: To prevent secrets from flowing from a high classification level to a low one, the {b1} model forbids reading up and writing down. If the main concern is keeping trusted data accurate, the {b2} model forbids reading down and writing up. A model that forces changes through approved transactions with separation of duties is {b3}.

options: Brewer-Nash
Bell-LaPadula
Biba
Biba
Bell-LaPadula
Brewer-Nash
Bell-LaPadula
Biba
Clark-Wilson

madlibs.explanation: Bell-LaPadula is the confidentiality model, Biba is the integrity model with the opposite rules, and Clark-Wilson is the commercial integrity model built on well-formed transactions, separation of duties and auditing.

madlibs.scenario: Network administrators need to authenticate to routers using a protocol over TCP that encrypts the entire payload and separates authentication, authorization and accounting; that protocol is {b1}. A protocol that runs over UDP and encrypts only the password is {b2}. For a site-to-site VPN that must provide confidentiality, IPsec should use {b3} in tunnel mode.

options: TACACS+
RADIUS
Kerberos
TACACS+
LDAPS
RADIUS
ICMP
ESP
AH

madlibs.explanation: TACACS+ is the device-administration protocol that encrypts the whole payload over TCP. RADIUS is UDP-based and protects only the password. ESP provides confidentiality as well as integrity, whereas AH authenticates without encrypting.

madlibs.scenario: A user types a password and then answers a security question; because both are things the user knows, this is {b1} authentication. A second company lets employees prove identity with a password plus a hardware token, which is {b2} authentication because the factors come from two different categories.

options: single-factor
multi-factor
biometric
single-factor
multi-factor
federated

madlibs.explanation: Multi-factor means at least two different categories (know, have, are). A password and a security question are both knowledge, so that is single-factor; a password plus a token spans know and have.

madlibs.scenario: A mobile app needs to read a user's calendar without ever receiving the password, so it requests a scoped access token using {b1}. The same app also wants a verifiable statement of who signed in, which is added by {b2}.

options: OAuth 2.0
RADIUS
Kerberos
TACACS+
OpenID Connect
LDAP

madlibs.explanation: OAuth 2.0 delegates limited access with tokens, which is authorization. OpenID Connect adds an ID token on top so the app can authenticate the user.

madlibs.scenario: A hospital can tolerate losing at most 30 minutes of transactions, which is its {b1}, and must restore service within four hours, which is its {b2}. The four hours plus the time to verify data must still fit inside the {b3}.

options: RPO
RTO
MTD
RPO
RTO
MTD
RPO
RTO
MTD

madlibs.explanation: RPO is acceptable data loss measured in time, RTO is the target time to restore, and MTD is the outer limit of downtime that the RTO and work recovery time must fit within.

madlibs.scenario: A customer wants proof that a cloud provider's controls operated effectively over twelve months, so it asks for a {b1} report. A scanner lists a vulnerability that turns out not to exist, which is a {b2}.

options: SOC 2 Type II
SOC 2 Type I
SOC 3
false negative
false positive
true positive

madlibs.explanation: A Type II report tests operating effectiveness over a period, while a Type I report only covers design on one date. A reported problem that is not real is a false positive.

madlibs.scenario: To stop attackers changing a database query through user input, developers should use {b1}. To stop attacker script running in other visitors' browsers, they should apply contextual {b2}.

options: parameterized queries
longer passwords
client-side checks
output encoding
database encryption
session timeouts

madlibs.explanation: Parameterized queries separate code from data to prevent SQL injection, and encoding output for its context prevents cross-site scripting.

sequences.prompt: Put the steps of the NIST Risk Management Framework (SP 800-37 Rev. 2) in the correct order.
steps: Prepare the organization and system for risk management
Categorize the system by impact
Select the security controls
Implement the controls
Assess the controls
Authorize the system to operate
Monitor the controls and the system continuously
sequences.explanation: The steps are Prepare, Categorize, Select, Implement, Assess, Authorize and Monitor. You must know the impact level before you can pick appropriate controls, and controls must be in place before they can be assessed. The authorizing official accepts residual risk only after the assessment, and monitoring then continues for the life of the system.

sequences.prompt: Order the main stages of business continuity and disaster recovery planning from start to finish.
steps: Obtain senior management support and define the scope of the plan
Conduct the business impact analysis
Identify preventive controls and choose recovery strategies
Develop the continuity and recovery plans
Train staff and test the plans
Maintain and update the plans as the business changes
sequences.explanation: Management support and scope come first, then the BIA identifies what is critical and sets recovery targets. Strategies such as alternate sites are chosen to meet those targets, the plans are written, then tested and taught, and kept current because an out-of-date plan fails when it is needed.

sequences.prompt: Place the stages of the information lifecycle in order.
steps: Create or collect the data
Store the data securely
Use the data
Share the data with authorized parties
Archive the data for its retention period
Securely destroy the data
sequences.explanation: Data is created or collected, stored, used and shared, archived while retention requirements apply and finally destroyed. Classification applies from creation and the controls follow the data through every stage; destruction is the stage most often neglected.

sequences.prompt: Order the steps in issuing and using a public key certificate.
steps: The subscriber generates a key pair and a certificate signing request
The registration authority verifies the requester's identity
The certificate authority signs the certificate with its own private key
The certificate is installed and published
Relying parties validate the chain of trust and check revocation status
The certificate is renewed at expiry or revoked if the key is compromised
sequences.explanation: The private key is created by the subscriber and never leaves them; only the public key goes into the request. Identity is verified before the authority signs, and anyone relying on the certificate validates the chain and checks CRL or OCSP before trusting it. A compromised key means revocation, not waiting for expiry.

sequences.prompt: Put the phases of incident response in the order they should occur.
steps: Preparation: build the plan, team and tools
Detection and analysis: confirm and scope the incident
Containment: limit spread while preserving evidence
Eradication: remove the cause and access
Recovery: restore systems and monitor for reinfection
Post-incident review: capture lessons and track improvements
sequences.explanation: Preparation comes first because it must exist before an incident. Containment precedes eradication so the problem stops spreading, and eradication precedes recovery so you do not restore into a compromised environment. Lessons learned closes the loop.

sequences.prompt: Order these evidence collection steps on a running suspect server, following the order of volatility and sound forensic practice.
steps: Photograph and document the scene and the system state
Capture memory and running process information
Record network connections and temporary data
Create a write-blocked bit-for-bit disk image
Verify the image by comparing hash values to the original
Log each transfer on the chain-of-custody form and store the original securely
sequences.explanation: Documenting first records the state before changes. Volatile data (memory, then network state) is collected before disk because it disappears fastest. The disk is imaged through a write blocker, verified by hashes, and custody is tracked from the beginning to the end.

sequences.prompt: Put the steps of a normal (non-emergency) change management process in order.
steps: Submit a change request with justification and rollback plan
Assess impact and security risk
Obtain approval from the change authority
Test and schedule the change
Implement the change
Verify the result and update documentation and baselines
sequences.explanation: A change is requested, assessed, approved, tested and scheduled before it is implemented, and then verified and documented so baselines stay accurate. Emergency changes compress the approval but still record and review afterwards.

sequences.prompt: Order the steps of Kerberos authentication to reach a file server for the first time.
steps: The user proves identity to the Authentication Service in the Key Distribution Center
The Authentication Service issues a ticket-granting ticket
The user presents the ticket-granting ticket to the Ticket-Granting Service for the file server
The Ticket-Granting Service issues a service ticket
The user presents the service ticket to the file server, which grants access
sequences.explanation: Identity is proven once to get a ticket-granting ticket, which is then exchanged for a service ticket for a specific resource, and only that service ticket is presented to the server. The password is not sent to the file server.

caseStudies.title: Meridian Family Clinics Moves Scheduling to a Cloud Vendor
caseStudies.scenario: Meridian Family Clinics operates 14 outpatient clinics in the United States and a telehealth service that also treats patients who live in EU member states. Leadership wants to replace its aging on-premises appointment system with a cloud vendor that will store patient names, appointment reasons and insurance details. The business impact analysis shows that clinics can work on paper for at most six hours before patient safety is affected, and that no more than 20 minutes of appointment changes can be lost. The vendor's standard contract has no breach notification terms and no audit rights, and the vendor says its security is 'industry leading' without providing evidence. The CIO proposes signing quickly to meet a discount deadline and says the team can discuss security after go-live. Separately, the compliance office has learned that a patient has threatened to sue over a past privacy incident, while a routine records purge of closed accounts is scheduled for next week.

questions.question: What is the BEST action regarding the vendor's contract before signing?
options: Negotiate security requirements, breach notification, a data protection agreement and a right-to-audit clause before go-live
Sign the standard contract now to secure the discount, then review the vendor's security and terms after go-live
Accept the vendor's statement that its security is industry leading and record it in the risk register as mitigated
Restrict the vendor to storing appointment times only, and skip the contract review because the data is lower risk
questions.explanation: Obligations that are not in the contract cannot be enforced, and the clinic remains accountable for patient data under HIPAA and, for EU patients, GDPR. Signing first and reviewing later gives away negotiating leverage. A vendor's unsupported claim is not evidence and cannot support marking a risk as mitigated, and limiting the data without contract terms still leaves the remaining data unprotected.

questions.question: Based on the BIA, which recovery objectives should the vendor's service level agreement meet for the appointment system?
options: An RTO comfortably inside six hours, and an RPO of no more than 20 minutes
An RTO of 24 hours and an RPO of 24 hours because the system is only for scheduling
An RTO of six hours and an RPO of six hours so that the two values match
An RTO of 20 minutes and an RPO of six hours
questions.explanation: The six-hour figure is the tolerable downtime, so the restore target plus verification time must fall within it, and the 20-minute figure is the tolerable data loss, which sets the recovery point. The other combinations swap the two measures or allow far more downtime or data loss than the business can tolerate.

questions.question: What should the records manager do about the scheduled purge of closed accounts?
options: Suspend deletion of relevant records under a legal hold until counsel says otherwise
Run the purge as scheduled, because it follows the written retention policy approved by the board
Run the purge but keep a copy of the deleted records on an administrator's laptop in case anyone asks for them
Run the purge and tell the patient that the records no longer exist
questions.explanation: Litigation is reasonably anticipated, so relevant records must be preserved even though a routine schedule says to delete them. Deleting them, even with a private copy, risks spoliation and breaks control of the data, and telling the patient the records are gone would be dishonest as well.

questions.question: Because the vendor will host the data, the clinics transfer their accountability for protecting patient data to the vendor.
questions.explanation: Outsourcing a function does not outsource accountability. The clinic, as the covered entity or controller, remains responsible for the data and must perform due diligence and oversight of the vendor.

caseStudies.title: Harborview Engineering Rebuilds a Flat Network
caseStudies.scenario: Harborview Engineering is a 400-person design firm whose network is a single flat segment. Its public web portal runs on the same switches as the file servers that hold client drawings. After a contractor's infected laptop scanned the network, leadership approved a security redesign. Administrators currently manage switches over Telnet, and the office Wi-Fi uses one WPA2 passphrase shared by everyone, including former contractors. Remote engineers use a full-tunnel VPN that gives access to every internal subnet. Clients have also received invoices that appear to come from Harborview's domain but were sent by criminals. The architect proposes a screened subnet for the portal, separate zones for engineering data and the corporate network, SSH for management, individual credentials for Wi-Fi, and email authentication for the domain. Engineers also work from client sites and home offices. The CIO asks which of these changes address the biggest exposures and how to improve remote access without slowing engineers down.

questions.question: Which change BEST limits how far a compromised web portal or infected laptop can move?
options: Segment into zones with least-privilege firewall rules between them, plus a screened subnet for the portal
Raising the Wi-Fi passphrase to 40 characters and rotating it each quarter
Installing a more powerful switch at the network core to carry the additional traffic
Moving the web portal to a different VLAN on the same switches, with open routing between all of the VLANs
questions.explanation: Segmentation with enforced rules between zones limits lateral movement, and a screened subnet keeps the internet-facing portal away from internal data. A longer passphrase and a faster switch do not control traffic between hosts, and a VLAN with open routing provides no real boundary.

questions.question: Which wireless change BEST addresses the problem of former contractors who still know the shared passphrase?
options: WPA3 or WPA2-Enterprise with 802.1X and individually revocable credentials
Hiding the network name so that former contractors can no longer see or reach it
Adding MAC address filtering to the access points and keeping the same passphrase
Changing the passphrase every month and emailing the new one to all staff and contractors
questions.explanation: Individual credentials let the company revoke one person's access and attribute activity. A hidden SSID and MAC filter are easily bypassed by anyone who has the passphrase, and rotating a shared passphrase that is emailed to everyone leaves the same weakness each time.

questions.question: Which TWO measures should the architect deploy to stop criminals from sending email that falsely appears to come from the firm's domain? (Choose two.)
options: SPF records listing authorized mail servers
DKIM message signing with a DMARC policy published for the domain
TLS on the web portal only
SNMPv3 on the mail servers
questions.explanation: SPF identifies which servers may send for the domain, and DKIM signing with a DMARC policy lets receivers verify messages and reject failures. TLS on the portal and SNMPv3 on the mail servers protect other things and do nothing to prevent domain spoofing.

questions.question: Replacing Telnet with SSH for switch management protects administrator credentials from being read on the network.
questions.explanation: Telnet sends credentials and commands in clear text, while SSH encrypts the session and can be combined with strong authentication and a dedicated management network.

caseStudies.title: Harbor Health Systems: Too Many Accounts After the Merger
caseStudies.scenario: Harbor Health Systems merged with a smaller regional clinic group last year. Staff now use about 50 applications, some on premises and some cloud-based, and sign in through three separate directories. The helpdesk reports that forgotten passwords are its largest ticket category. An internal audit has also found several problems: 35 former contractors still have active accounts in the scheduling application, a nurse manager who transferred from pediatrics to billing still holds clinical record permissions, and the network team administers routers using one shared password stored in a spreadsheet. The chief information security officer wants a plan that reduces passwords, enforces multi-factor authentication consistently, fixes the lifecycle failures and gives administrators individual accountability. A pilot application used by physicians on tablets needs to let users sign in with their hospital identity and verify who they are, while a partner research portal needs to read a limited set of data from the hospital's records service on a physician's behalf. The budget is limited, so the plan should favor standards over custom code.

questions.question: Which strategy BEST addresses the helpdesk load and the inconsistent multi-factor authentication?
options: Federate applications to one identity provider with SSO and enforce MFA there
Let each application owner choose its own authentication method and password rules
Reduce the password length requirement so users forget fewer characters
Create one shared account per department for application access
questions.explanation: A central identity provider with SSO cuts the number of passwords and gives one place to enforce MFA and conditional policy. Letting owners choose keeps the fragmentation, shorter passwords weaken security, and shared accounts destroy accountability.

questions.question: Which TWO findings point to failures in the leaver and mover steps of the identity lifecycle, and what is the BEST single fix for both?
options: Former contractors and the transferred manager; automate changes from the HR record and add access reviews
The shared router password and the three directories; buy a larger firewall to protect the network
The helpdesk ticket volume and the tablet pilot; lengthen password expiry across all applications
The partner portal and the physician tablets; remove all single sign-on from the environment
questions.explanation: Active accounts for former contractors are a leaver failure, and retained clinical permissions after a transfer are a mover failure (privilege creep). Linking account changes to the authoritative HR source, with automation and recertification, addresses the cause. The other options match the wrong findings or offer unrelated controls.

questions.question: Which two standards should the team use for the physician tablet sign-in and for the partner portal's delegated read access? (Choose two.)
options: OpenID Connect for signing in physicians with the hospital identity and obtaining an ID token
OAuth 2.0 for issuing the partner portal a scoped access token to the records service
RADIUS for authorizing the partner portal's API calls
LDAP simple binds over unencrypted connections for the tablets
A shared service account whose password is embedded in the portal
questions.explanation: OpenID Connect authenticates the user in the mobile app, and OAuth 2.0 delegates limited access to an API without sharing the password. RADIUS is for network access, unencrypted LDAP exposes credentials, and an embedded shared password is both insecure and unattributable.

questions.question: Which control BEST fixes the shared router password problem while giving each network administrator individual accountability?
options: Move the shared password into a more complex format and keep the spreadsheet encrypted
A privileged access management vault with check-out, session recording and TACACS+
Post a policy reminding all administrators not to share the password with outsiders
Give every network administrator permanent enterprise-wide administrator rights
questions.explanation: PAM replaces the shared secret with brokered, attributed, recorded access, and TACACS+ gives per-command authorization and accounting on devices. A complex shared password is still shared, reminders are unenforceable, and permanent broad rights are the opposite of least privilege.

caseStudies.title: Northwind Logistics: Ransomware on a Tuesday Night
caseStudies.scenario: Northwind Logistics runs warehouse management on a cluster of servers, and the business has set an RTO of six hours and an RPO of one hour for it. At 02:10 the security monitoring platform raises an alert that a file server is encrypting files, and by 02:25 two more servers show the same behavior. The on-call analyst confirms an incident and wakes the response team. The team lead, a network engineer, proposes powering off all affected servers immediately, while the legal counsel asks that evidence be preserved because the company may need to report the incident to a regulator and cyber insurer. Investigation shows the entry point was a phished administrator credential used on a remote access gateway without MFA. Backups are taken nightly to a share that the same administrator account can write to. The backup operator reports that an additional immutable cloud copy is replicated every 30 minutes. Leadership asks the team to restore operations quickly but wants a clear explanation afterward of what failed and what will change. The log servers are in a separate management network and were not affected.

questions.question: What is the BEST immediate action for the affected servers, considering both stopping the spread and preserving evidence?
options: Power them all off immediately to stop the encryption from spreading further
Isolate them from the network, keep them powered on and capture memory first
Reboot all servers into safe mode and run a cleanup tool on each of them
Delete the encrypted files and restore them from the nightly backup share
questions.explanation: Network isolation stops lateral spread while keeping volatile evidence such as memory, which may hold keys or attacker artifacts, available for capture before imaging. Powering off destroys that evidence, rebooting changes the state, and deleting files and restoring from a reachable share risks loss of both evidence and clean data.

questions.question: Which backup source should the team use to restore, given the stated RPO and the situation?
options: The nightly backup share, because it is the most commonly used copy
Any available copy, because all copies are equally trustworthy after the attack
The immutable cloud copy, once confirmed to predate the infection
No backups; rebuild all of the data by hand from paper records
questions.explanation: The immutable copy is protected from the compromised credentials and replicates every 30 minutes, which fits the one-hour RPO. The nightly share was writable by the compromised account and could be encrypted or tampered with, and a nightly copy would also miss the RPO. Rebuilding by hand would not meet the RTO.

questions.question: Which two actions belong in the eradication and recovery work before systems return to service? (Choose two.)
options: Remove the attacker's access by resetting the compromised credentials and closing the unprotected remote gateway path with MFA
Rebuild affected servers from known-good images and restore data from a verified clean copy, with heightened monitoring afterward
Return servers to the network first and scan them while users work
Disable logging to reduce noise during recovery
Reuse the compromised administrator account for the restoration
questions.explanation: Eradication must remove the cause and the access path, and recovery must rebuild from trusted sources and watch for reinfection. Reconnecting before verification invites reinfection, disabling logging blinds the team, and reusing the compromised account keeps the attacker's door open.

questions.question: True or false: the post-incident review should concentrate on identifying which administrator to discipline rather than on the missing MFA and the backup design.
questions.explanation: Lessons-learned reviews are blameless and focus on root causes and control improvements: MFA on remote access, privileged credential handling and protecting backups from the same credentials. Focusing on blame discourages reporting and does not fix the systemic weaknesses.

compare.scenario: After controls are applied, the residual risk to the company's main revenue system still exceeds the risk appetite set by the board. What is the better next step?
compare.optionA: The security manager formally accepts the residual risk because the technical team understands it best.
compare.optionB: The security manager reports the gap to the risk owner and senior management for a treatment decision.
compare.why: Risk acceptance belongs to the business owner or senior management who control the budget and bear the consequences. Security informs and recommends. Accepting the risk themselves is the tempting runner-up because the security team has the technical knowledge, but expertise does not confer the authority to accept risk on the organization's behalf.

compare.scenario: A company is starting its first disaster recovery project and wants to protect the order system quickly after a recent outage. What should the team do first?
compare.optionA: Contract a hot site so that the order system can fail over within minutes.
compare.optionB: Conduct a business impact analysis with business owners to establish recovery priorities and targets.
compare.why: Recovery strategies must be driven by requirements that the BIA produces (MTD, RTO and RPO). The hot site is the tempting runner-up because it feels like decisive action, but it may overspend on one system, ignore more critical processes, or still miss a data-loss target.

compare.scenario: A company must resell a batch of retired solid-state drives that held confidential customer data and which were encrypted with strong keys from first use. Which approach is better?
compare.optionA: Degauss the drives and send them to the reseller with a certificate of degaussing.
compare.optionB: Perform a cryptographic erase by destroying the keys, verify it, then release the drives.
compare.why: Cryptographic erase is a valid purge for encrypted flash media and lets the drives be reused. Degaussing is the tempting runner-up because it is the classic answer for hard drives, but it has no effect on solid-state memory, so the data would remain.

compare.scenario: A certificate authority's root signing key must be protected against theft by both outsiders and insiders. Which is the better design?
compare.optionA: Store the key in a hardware security module kept offline, with dual control for any use.
compare.optionB: Store the key on an encrypted file server protected by a strong password known to two administrators.
compare.why: A tamper-resistant offline HSM with dual control keeps the key from ever being exposed and prevents a single person from using it. The encrypted file server is the tempting runner-up because it uses encryption and two people, but the key can be copied off the server and is exposed whenever the password holders log in.

compare.scenario: A hospital pharmacy system receives dosage data from many sources. The main concern is that low-trust sources must never be able to alter high-trust dosage records. Which model is the better fit?
compare.optionA: Biba, which prevents reading from lower integrity levels and writing to higher ones.
compare.optionB: Bell-LaPadula, which prevents reading higher classification data and writing to lower levels.
compare.why: The concern is integrity, which is the purpose of Biba. Bell-LaPadula is the tempting runner-up because it also uses levels and no-read, no-write rules, but those rules protect confidentiality of classified data and do not stop low-trust data from contaminating high-trust records.

compare.scenario: An office's wireless network uses one WPA2 passphrase shared by all 300 employees, and staff turnover is high. Which change is better?
compare.optionA: Switch to WPA3 or WPA2 Enterprise using 802.1X with individual credentials.
compare.optionB: Keep the shared passphrase but make it 30 characters long and change it every quarter.
compare.why: Individual credentials let you attribute activity and revoke one person when they leave. A long passphrase is the tempting runner-up because it resists guessing, but everyone still shares it, so departures, accountability and quarterly rotation across 300 devices remain unsolved.

compare.scenario: Remote employees use a VPN to reach internal applications. The security team is concerned that compromised home computers could reach any internal system and also that internet traffic is not inspected. Which is the better approach?
compare.optionA: Keep full-tunnel VPN access and add a zero trust network access layer that grants per-application access after verifying identity and device posture.
compare.optionB: Enable split tunneling and install a stronger antivirus product on all remote laptops.
compare.why: Per-application access reduces lateral movement, and full tunnel keeps traffic under corporate inspection. Split tunneling with antivirus is the tempting runner-up because it addresses endpoint infection, but it removes visibility of internet traffic and leaves broad network access in place.

compare.scenario: A company wants to host a public web server and keep a compromise of it from reaching internal databases. Which is the better design?
compare.optionA: Place the web server in a separate VLAN on the internal switches with no firewall between that VLAN and the database VLAN.
compare.optionB: Place the web server in a screened subnet with firewall rules allowing only the specific application traffic to the database.
compare.why: A screened subnet with firewalls enforces boundary control and limits what a compromised server can reach. The separate VLAN is the tempting runner-up because VLANs do separate broadcast domains, but without access controls between the VLANs it provides no real security boundary.

compare.scenario: A defense contractor wants engineers to open a design file only when the file carries a project tag, the engineer is assigned to that project, the device passes a health check and the request comes from an approved country. Which access control approach is the better answer?
compare.optionA: Role-based access control, with a separate role created for each project, device state and country combination.
compare.optionB: Attribute-based access control, with a policy that evaluates the file tag, user assignment, device health and location at request time.
compare.why: The decision depends on several contextual attributes at once, which attribute-based control evaluates directly. Role-based control is the tempting runner-up because it is familiar and simple, but expressing device health and location through roles would explode into an unmanageable number of roles and could not react to changes at request time.

compare.scenario: A company's administrators are being targeted by phishing sites that mimic the admin portal. Which authentication method is the better choice to protect those accounts?
compare.optionA: FIDO2 hardware security keys whose credentials only work on the genuine site.
compare.optionB: A six-digit code sent by text message after the password is entered.
compare.why: FIDO2 credentials are bound to the real site and cannot be replayed on a look-alike page, so phishing fails. Text message codes are the tempting runner-up because they are an extra factor and easy to roll out, but a phishing proxy can capture and relay them in real time, and the number can also be intercepted or swapped.

compare.scenario: A new mobile application must let employees sign in with their corporate identity, and the app must receive a verifiable statement of who signed in. Which standard is the better fit?
compare.optionA: SAML 2.0, with XML assertions posted through a browser redirect.
compare.optionB: OpenID Connect, with an ID token obtained through an OAuth 2.0 flow.
compare.why: OpenID Connect was designed for modern web and mobile sign-in and returns an ID token the app can verify. SAML is the tempting runner-up because it is the established enterprise single sign-on standard, but its browser-centric XML flows are awkward for native mobile apps, which makes OpenID Connect the better fit here.

compare.scenario: The security manager must report weekly on missing patches across 2,000 internal servers at the lowest cost. Which activity is the better choice?
compare.optionA: Credentialed vulnerability scans run weekly with results validated and trended.
compare.optionB: A full-scope penetration test run by an outside firm every week.
compare.why: Credentialed scans inspect patch levels accurately across many hosts at low cost and can run automatically. A penetration test is the tempting runner-up because it sounds more rigorous, but it is slow, expensive and aimed at demonstrating exploitation paths, not enumerating missing patches across thousands of systems every week.

compare.scenario: A listed company needs credible assurance for its regulator that its security controls are effective. Which review is the better choice?
compare.optionA: An audit by an independent external firm against a recognized standard.
compare.optionB: A thorough assessment performed by the company's own security team.
compare.why: Independence gives an outside audit credibility with regulators. The internal assessment is the tempting runner-up because the team knows the environment and it is cheaper, and it is excellent for readiness, but it lacks the independence needed to convince third parties.

compare.scenario: A file server is restored every Sunday from a full backup. The team wants the fastest possible restore on any other day while keeping each daily backup reasonably small. Which scheme is the better choice?
compare.optionA: Daily differential backups after the Sunday full backup.
compare.optionB: Daily incremental backups after the Sunday full backup.
compare.why: A differential restore needs only the last full backup plus the most recent differential, so recovery is fast and simple. Incremental backups are the tempting runner-up because each daily job is smallest, but a restore must apply the full backup and every incremental in order, which is slower and more fragile.

compare.scenario: A responder has found an active intrusion on a server that may be needed in a criminal case. Which action is the better first move?
compare.optionA: Pull the power cable to stop the attacker immediately.
compare.optionB: Isolate the server from the network, then capture memory and running state before imaging the disk.
compare.why: Isolation stops the attacker's reach while keeping volatile evidence intact for collection in order of volatility. Pulling the power is the tempting runner-up because it feels like the decisive way to stop the attack, but it destroys memory contents and running-process information that may be essential evidence.

compare.scenario: A development team wants security feedback on each commit, before a runnable test build exists, and pointing to the exact line of vulnerable code. Which testing approach is the better choice?
compare.optionA: Dynamic application security testing against a deployed test environment.
compare.optionB: Static application security testing integrated into the commit pipeline.
compare.why: Static analysis reads the code itself, needs no running application, and reports the file and line involved, so it fits early feedback in the pipeline. Dynamic testing is the tempting runner-up because it finds real runtime flaws, but it needs a deployed build and cannot point to the offending line, so it comes later.
